micro_skills.micro_skill: Disk method
definitions: The disk method finds the volume of a solid formed by rotating a region 0 ≤ y ≤ f(x), a ≤ x ≤ b about the x-axis (the region's own lower boundary), by summing circular disk cross-sections of radius f(x) and thickness dx.

theorems.name: Volume by disks (rotation about the x-axis)
theorems.statement: If f is continuous and f(x) ≥ 0 on [a,b], and R is the region 0 ≤ y ≤ f(x), a ≤ x ≤ b, rotated about the x-axis, then V = π∫[a,b] [f(x)]^2 dx.
conditions: f continuous on [a,b]
f(x) ≥ 0 on [a,b]
axis of rotation is the boundary y = 0 of the region (no gap)

formulas: V = π∫[c,d] [g(y)]^2 dy  (rotate about y-axis, x = g(y))

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the volume generated by rotating the region bounded by y=f(x), y=0, x=a, x=b about the x-axis.
question_archetypes.example: Rotate y=√x, 0≤x≤4, about the x-axis.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The region's lower boundary is already y=0 and rotation is about that same x-axis — no gap between curve and axis.
method_plan: Confirm the region touches the axis of rotation
Identify radius = f(x)
Set up V=π∫[a,b][f(x)]^2 dx
Evaluate the integral
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct radius identified as f(x)
M1: correct integral V=π∫f(x)^2 dx with correct limits
A1: correct antiderivative/evaluation
A1: correct final answer

common_errors.description: Using the disk formula when the region does not actually touch the axis of rotation (should be a washer)
Squaring f(x) incorrectly, e.g. forgetting to square a radical properly
Dropping the factor of π

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the volume generated by rotating a region about the y-axis using x=g(y) and disks.
question_archetypes.example: Rotate the region bounded by x=y^2, x=0, 0≤y≤2 about the y-axis.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Rotation axis is vertical (y-axis) and the boundary curve is naturally solved for x in terms of y.
method_plan: Rewrite the boundary curve as x=g(y)
Identify radius = g(y)
Set up V=π∫[c,d][g(y)]^2 dy
Evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly solved for x=g(y)
M1: correct integral setup with y-limits
A1: correct integration
A1: correct final answer

common_errors.description: Forgetting to convert both the equation and the limits from the x-variable to the y-variable
Errors solving for x in terms of y
Mixing dx and dy notation in the final integral

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Derive the volume of a standard solid (ball, cone) by rotating a known curve using disks.
question_archetypes.example: Find the volume of a ball of radius a by rotating y=√(a^2-x^2), -a≤x≤a, about the x-axis.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The prompt names a classical solid (sphere, cone, ellipsoid) generated by a recognizable curve rotated about an axis.
method_plan: Identify the generating curve and axis
Use symmetry to halve the interval if convenient
Set up and evaluate the disk integral
Check the result against the known closed-form volume
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct setup exploiting symmetry
A1: correct antiderivative
A1: correct evaluation matching the known volume formula
M1: justification of limits/symmetry

common_errors.description: Sign or expansion errors in (a^2-x^2)
Not using symmetry, doing twice the necessary integration work
Not simplifying the final answer to the standard closed form

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the (possibly finite) volume of an infinite solid of revolution using an improper integral with the disk method.
question_archetypes.example: Find the volume generated by rotating y=1/x, x≥1, about the x-axis (Gabriel's horn).
question_archetypes.answer: V=π∫[1,∞) dx/x^2 = π·lim(R→∞)[-1/x] from 1 to R = π
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The region of revolution extends to infinity (unbounded interval or vertical asymptote) — a definite integral with an infinite limit or discontinuous integrand.
method_plan: Set up the disk integral with the infinite limit
Rewrite as lim(R→∞)∫[1,R]
Evaluate the proper integral in terms of R
Take the limit and state convergence
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly rewrote as a limit of a proper integral
A1: correct antiderivative
A1: correct limit evaluation and convergence conclusion
presentation: noting finite volume despite infinite region if relevant

common_errors.description: Plugging in ∞ directly instead of taking a limit
Assuming an infinite region must always give infinite volume
Sign error evaluating the antiderivative at the lower limit

micro_skills.micro_skill: Washer method
definitions: The washer method finds the volume of a solid formed by rotating a region between two curves f(x) (outer) ≥ g(x) (inner) ≥ 0 about an axis, by summing annular cross-sections (washers) with outer radius f(x) and inner radius g(x).

theorems.name: Volume by washers
theorems.statement: If f(x) ≥ g(x) ≥ 0 on [a,b] and the region between them is rotated about the x-axis, V = π∫[a,b]([f(x)]^2-[g(x)]^2) dx.
conditions: f, g continuous on [a,b]
outer and inner radii measured from the actual axis of rotation, not necessarily from y=0
axis of rotation does not pass through the interior of the region

formulas: outer radius = (outer boundary value) − (axis location); inner radius = (inner boundary value) − (axis location)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the volume generated by rotating the region between two curves y=f(x) and y=g(x) about the x-axis.
question_archetypes.example: Rotate the region between y=√x and y=x, 0≤x≤1, about the x-axis.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Two curves bound the region and the axis of rotation is a line the region does not touch — there is a gap between the region and the axis.
method_plan: Find intersection points for the limits
Identify outer curve (farther from axis) and inner curve
Set up π∫(outer^2-inner^2)dx
Evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct intersection limits
M1: correct outer/inner identification
A1: correct integral setup
A1: correct evaluation

common_errors.description: Swapping outer and inner radius, giving a negative or wrong volume
Using (f-g)^2 instead of f^2-g^2
Error finding intersection points

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the volume generated by rotating a region about a horizontal (or vertical) line that does not coincide with either boundary curve.
question_archetypes.example: Rotate the region bounded by y=x^2 and y=4 about the line y=-1.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The axis of rotation is a line other than the coordinate axis the region touches — radii must be recomputed as (boundary value − axis value).
method_plan: Determine axis location y=k
Compute outer radius = outer curve − k, inner radius = inner curve − k
Set up the washer integral
Evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct radii relative to the shifted axis
M1: correct limits
A1: correct integral
A1: correct evaluation

common_errors.description: Measuring radius from y=0 instead of from the actual axis of rotation
Sign error subtracting a negative axis value
Not expanding the squared binomial correctly before integrating

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the volume generated by rotating a region between two curves about the y-axis using washers with x=g(y).
question_archetypes.example: Rotate the region between x=y and x=y^2, 0≤y≤1, about the y-axis.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Rotation is about the y-axis and the region is naturally described with x=g(y) for both boundaries.
method_plan: Express both boundary curves as x=g(y)
Determine which is outer/inner in y
Set up π∫(outer^2-inner^2)dy
Evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct outer/inner in y
M1: correct limits
A1: correct integral
A1: correct evaluation

common_errors.description: Failing to convert curves given as y=f(x) into x=g(y) form first
Swapping outer/inner because y ≥ y^2 intuition from x-form doesn't transfer directly
Errors solving for x in terms of y

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the volume generated by rotating about an axis a region bounded by two curves that cross within the interval, requiring the integral to be split.
question_archetypes.example: Rotate the region between y=sin x and y=cos x, 0≤x≤π/2, about the x-axis.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The two bounding curves cross within the given interval, so which curve is 'outer' switches partway through — a single formula across the whole interval is wrong.
method_plan: Find the crossing point(s) by solving f(x)=g(x)
Split the interval at the crossing
Determine outer/inner on each sub-interval separately
Sum the two washer integrals
full_mark_rubric: M1: found the crossing point
M1: correct outer/inner assignment on each piece
A1: correct integral setup for each piece
A1: correct sum/evaluation

common_errors.description: Not noticing the curves swap order and using one washer formula across the entire interval
Forgetting to split the integral at the crossing point
Errors solving sin x = cos x (or similar) for the crossing point

micro_skills.micro_skill: Cylindrical shells
definitions: The shell method finds the volume of a solid of revolution by summing thin cylindrical shells swept out by a strip parallel to the axis of rotation: a vertical strip of height f(x), width dx, at distance x (radius) from the y-axis sweeps out a shell of volume dV=2πx f(x) dx.

theorems.name: Volume by shells
theorems.statement: If the region 0≤y≤f(x), 0≤a<x<b is rotated about the y-axis, V=2π∫[a,b] x f(x) dx.
conditions: f continuous on [a,b]
strip used is parallel to the axis of rotation
a ≥ 0 so radius x is nonnegative

formulas: V=2π∫[a,b] x f(x) dx  (rotate about y-axis, vertical strips)
V=2π∫[c,d] y g(y) dy  (rotate about x-axis, horizontal strips)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the volume generated by rotating a region about the y-axis using cylindrical shells with vertical strips.
question_archetypes.example: Rotate the region bounded by y=x^2, y=0, x=2 about the y-axis.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Rotation is about the y-axis and the curve is naturally given as y=f(x) — solving for x=g(y) would be awkward or impossible.
method_plan: Identify shell radius = x and shell height = f(x)
Set up V=2π∫x f(x)dx over the x-limits
Evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct radius and height identified
M1: correct integral setup with factor 2π
A1: correct antiderivative
A1: correct final answer

common_errors.description: Forgetting the factor of 2π (using π as in the disk method)
Using x as height and f(x) as radius (swapped)
Not simplifying before integrating

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the volume generated by rotating a region about the x-axis using cylindrical shells with horizontal strips.
question_archetypes.example: Rotate the region bounded by x=y^2, x=0, 0≤y≤2 about the x-axis.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Rotation is about the x-axis but the curve is naturally given as x=g(y), so a horizontal strip parallel to the x-axis is the efficient choice.
method_plan: Identify shell radius = y and shell height = g(y)
Set up V=2π∫y g(y)dy over the y-limits
Evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct radius/height identification in y
M1: correct integral with 2π factor
A1: correct antiderivative
A1: correct final answer

common_errors.description: Defaulting to the disk/washer method out of habit when shells with a y-strip are far simpler
Mixing up which variable is the radius vs. the height
Errors converting the curve to x=g(y) form

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the volume generated by rotating a region about a vertical (or horizontal) line other than the y-axis (or x-axis) using shells.
question_archetypes.example: The triangle bounded by y=x, y=0, x=a>0 is rotated about the line x=b>a.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The axis of rotation is shifted away from the coordinate axis, so the shell radius is (axis location − x) or (x − axis location), not simply x.
method_plan: Identify the shell height as before
Compute the shell radius as the distance from the strip to the actual axis of rotation
Set up V=2π∫(radius)(height)dx
Evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct radius expression relative to shifted axis
M1: correct height
A1: correct integral setup
A1: correct evaluation

common_errors.description: Using x as the radius even though the axis of rotation is not the y-axis
Sign error in (b-x) when the axis is to the right of the region
Not stating clearly which distance is the radius vs. height before integrating

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use cylindrical shells to find the volume of a solid of revolution generated by a region not touching the axis of rotation (e.g. a torus).
question_archetypes.example: A disk of radius a centred at (b,0), b>a>0, is rotated about the y-axis; find the volume of the resulting torus.
question_archetypes.answer: V = 4∫[b-a,b+a] x√(a^2-(x-b)^2) dx = 2π^2 a^2 b (via substitution u=x-b, odd part vanishes)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The generating region is entirely offset from the axis of rotation (does not touch it), producing a solid with a hole (torus-type solid).
method_plan: Set up the shell integral using the full height (upper minus lower boundary) at each x
Substitute u=x-b to centre the integral at 0
Split into odd and even parts; the odd part integrates to 0
Evaluate the remaining even part using a known area (e.g. semicircle)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct shell height as difference of two square-root boundaries
M1: correct substitution to simplify
A1: correctly discarding the odd-integrand term
A1: correct final evaluation, ideally cross-checked with Pappus's Theorem

common_errors.description: Not recognizing the substitution u=x-b simplifies the integral into odd+even parts
Forgetting the region has both an upper and lower boundary (the shell height is a difference, not a single function)
Grinding through the full integral instead of recognizing it can be checked instantly via Pappus's Theorem

micro_skills.micro_skill: Choosing disk/washer vs. shells and the strip orientation
definitions: The volume element is built by rotating an area strip about the axis: a strip perpendicular to the axis of rotation sweeps out a disk/washer; a strip parallel to the axis of rotation sweeps out a cylindrical shell. Choosing the right strip orientation (and hence method) before setting up any integral is the key strategic decision in every volume-of-revolution problem.

theorems.name: Strip-orientation rule
theorems.statement: A vertical strip (dx) rotated about a horizontal axis gives disks/washers; rotated about a vertical axis gives shells. A horizontal strip (dy) rotated about a vertical axis gives disks/washers; rotated about a horizontal axis gives shells.
conditions: applies to any planar region being rotated about a line in its own plane

formulas: strip ⟂ axis ⇒ disk/washer: dV=π(radius)^2 dx or dy
strip ∥ axis ⇒ shell: dV=2π(radius)(height) dx or dy

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a region and an axis of rotation, state (without integrating) whether disks/washers or shells are the natural choice, and why.
question_archetypes.example: Region bounded by y=x^3, y=8, x=0, rotated about the y-axis — which method is easiest?
question_archetypes.answer: Shells with vertical strips (dx): radius x, height (8-x^3); avoids solving y=x^3 for x.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: One of the two natural variable-solving directions (x=g(y) or y=f(x)) is algebraically messy or impossible — the other, easier direction dictates the method.
method_plan: Determine whether the curve is easier to express as y=f(x) or x=g(y)
Match strip orientation (dx or dy) to whichever form is natural
State whether that strip orientation is parallel or perpendicular to the axis
Name the resulting method (disk/washer or shell) without computing
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies which variable form is algebraically natural
M1: correctly matches strip orientation to axis to name the method
A1: brief justification referencing ease of solving for x or y

common_errors.description: Defaulting to disks/washers out of habit even when shells clearly avoid an algebraically painful inversion
Confusing which strip orientation is parallel vs. perpendicular to a given axis
Naming a method without justifying it in terms of the strip orientation

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Set up (but do not necessarily evaluate) the volume integral for the same region and axis using both disks/washers and shells, and confirm they would give the same answer.
question_archetypes.example: Region bounded by y=x^2 and y=2x rotated about the y-axis: set up both a washer integral (dy strips) and a shell integral (dx strips).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem explicitly asks for both setups, or the region/curves are simple enough that both inversions (x=g(y) and y=f(x)) are tractable — a good check-your-work scenario.
method_plan: Set up the shell integral using dx strips parallel to the axis
Set up the washer integral using dy strips perpendicular to the axis (requires solving for x in terms of y)
Evaluate both (or note they must agree) as a consistency check
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct shell setup
M1: correct washer setup requiring correct inversion to x=g(y)
A1: both integrals evaluated to the same numeric volume
presentation: clear labelling of which strip/method is used where

common_errors.description: Errors inverting y=x^2 or similar to x=√y when finding the washer form
Mismatched limits between the two setups (using x-limits in a dy integral or vice versa)
Not using the agreement of both answers as a check, missing a chance to catch an earlier error

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Identify and correct a flawed volume setup that used the wrong method or measured a radius incorrectly.
question_archetypes.example: A student rotates the region between y=x^2 and y=4, x≥0 about the x-axis and writes V=π∫[0,2] x^4 dx (using only the disk formula for y=x^2, ignoring y=4). Identify the error.
question_archetypes.answer: The region is not bounded below by y=0, so this must be a washer: outer radius 4 (from y=4), inner radius x^2 (from y=x^2); V=π∫[0,2](16-x^4)dx.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A worked (possibly flawed) volume setup is presented and the task is to check whether the region actually touches the axis and whether disk vs. washer was chosen correctly.
method_plan: Sketch or describe the region relative to the axis of rotation
Check whether the region touches the axis (disk) or has a gap (washer)
Recompute the correct radius/radii
Rewrite the corrected integral
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly diagnoses disk vs. washer error
M1: correctly identifies outer and inner radii
A1: corrected integral written
A1: correct evaluation of the corrected integral

common_errors.description: Using the disk formula π∫f^2 dx when the region does not touch the axis of rotation
Forgetting the factor of 2π when the correct method is actually shells
Not sketching the region, leading to a radius measured from the wrong reference line

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given only a picture (or verbal description) of a region and an axis, without any equations, decide the method and roughly describe the integral (recognition-only, no computation).
question_archetypes.example: A bounded region sits entirely to the right of the y-axis with a curved left edge and straight right edge; it is rotated about a horizontal line below the region. Which method, and why?
question_archetypes.answer: Washers with vertical (dx) strips perpendicular to the horizontal axis; radius measured from each curve down to the axis, not from y=0.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: No explicit formulas are given, only a geometric description — the decision must be made purely from the relative orientation of the region and axis.
method_plan: Determine the axis orientation (horizontal or vertical)
Determine whether a natural strip (dx or dy) would be parallel or perpendicular to that axis
Name disks/washers vs. shells accordingly
Note whether the region touches the axis (disk) or not (washer)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct axis-orientation reasoning
M1: correct strip-orientation to method mapping
A1: correct disk-vs-washer distinction based on gap to axis

common_errors.description: Trying to force an equation-based method before doing the qualitative geometric reasoning first
Mixing up which strip orientation is parallel to a given axis
Giving a method name with no reasoning tied to the picture

micro_skills.micro_skill: Volume from a known non-circular cross-sectional area function A(x)
definitions: If a solid lies between planes x=a and x=b and its cross-sectional area perpendicular to the x-axis at position x is the continuous function A(x) (not necessarily a disk/washer), then V=∫[a,b] A(x) dx.

theorems.name: General slicing formula
theorems.statement: V=∫[a,b] A(x) dx, where A(x) is the area of the cross-section perpendicular to the x-axis at position x.
conditions: A(x) continuous on [a,b]
cross-sections all taken perpendicular to the same fixed axis

formulas: square cross-section on base width w(x): A(x)=w(x)^2
equilateral triangle cross-section on base w(x): A(x)=(√3/4)w(x)^2
semicircular cross-section on diameter w(x): A(x)=(π/8)w(x)^2

question_archetypes.prompt_template: A solid has a given base region, and every cross-section perpendicular to a fixed axis is a square whose side equals the chord length of the base at that position. Find the volume.
question_archetypes.example: Base is the disk x^2+y^2≤4; cross-sections perpendicular to the x-axis are squares. Find V.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem states the cross-section shape (square, triangle, semicircle) explicitly and gives a base curve to supply the side length — not a solid of revolution.
method_plan: Express the side/base length of the cross-section as a function of the slicing variable
Write A(x) using the cross-section's area formula
Integrate A(x) over the base's extent
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct chord/side length as a function of x
M1: correct area formula for the named cross-section shape
A1: correct integral setup and limits
A1: correct evaluation

common_errors.description: Treating the solid as a solid of revolution and reaching for π(radius)^2 instead of the stated cross-section shape
Errors squaring or simplifying the chord-length expression
Not stating A(x) explicitly before integrating

question_archetypes.prompt_template: A solid has cross-sections perpendicular to an axis that are triangles (isosceles or right) with base and/or height given as functions of position. Find the volume.
question_archetypes.example: A tent has a circular base of radius a, a ridge at height b above a diameter, and cross-sections perpendicular to the ridge are isosceles triangles. Find V.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The cross-section is explicitly triangular and its base width comes from a circular (or other curved) footprint, requiring a standard area recognized (e.g. semicircle area) to finish the integral.
method_plan: Identify the triangle's base and height as functions of the slicing variable
Write A(x)=½·base·height
Integrate, using known area shortcuts (e.g. semicircle) where the integrand matches one
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct base and height expressions
M1: correct triangle area formula A(x)=½bh
A1: correct integral set up
A1: correct evaluation, ideally via a recognized standard-area shortcut

common_errors.description: Using the full base as if it were a rectangle (forgetting the ½ in triangle area)
Grinding out ∫√(a^2-x^2)dx by trig substitution instead of recognizing it as a semicircle's area
Sign or factoring slip under the square root

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the volume of a solid formed by the intersection of two solids (e.g. two perpendicular cylinders), using symmetry and a cross-section that is a simple polygon.
question_archetypes.example: Two cylinders of radius a with perpendicular axes intersect. Find the volume of the intersection (Steinmetz solid).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The solid is described as an intersection of two familiar solids with perpendicular axes — slicing perpendicular to the common axis of symmetry gives a simple polygonal (often square) cross-section.
method_plan: Choose the slicing axis to be the axis of symmetry shared by both cylinders
Determine the cross-section shape in one octant and its side length
Use symmetry to write the total volume as a multiple of the one-octant integral
Integrate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct cross-section shape and side length identified in one octant
M1: correct symmetry factor (e.g. ×8)
A1: correct integral setup
A1: correct evaluation

common_errors.description: Not exploiting symmetry, attempting to integrate over the full solid directly
Misidentifying the cross-section shape (assuming circular instead of square)
Errors in (a^2-z^2) expansion or evaluation

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Identify and correct a cross-sectional-area setup where the area function was left in terms of the wrong variable.
question_archetypes.example: A student slices a solid with base y=√x, 0≤x≤4, using square cross-sections perpendicular to the x-axis, but writes A(x)=y^2 without substituting y=√x. Identify and fix the error.
question_archetypes.answer: A(x) must be expressed purely in x: A(x)=(√x)^2=x, so V=∫[0,4]x dx=8
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The area expression still contains a variable (often y) that has not been eliminated using the boundary curve's equation — a mixed-variable A(x) cannot be integrated in x.
method_plan: Check whether A(x) is written purely in terms of the slicing variable
Substitute the boundary curve's equation to eliminate any other variable
Re-integrate with the corrected, single-variable A(x)
full_mark_rubric: M1: identifies the mixed-variable error
A1: correct substitution eliminating y
A1: correct corrected integral and evaluation

common_errors.description: Leaving cross-sectional area in terms of both x and y instead of one variable
Not realizing A(x) must be a pure function of the slicing variable before integrating
Not showing the substitution step explicitly

micro_skills.micro_skill: Pyramid/cone volume via similar-cross-section scaling (V=⅓Ah)
definitions: A pyramid or cone with base area A and height h has cross-sections parallel to the base, at distance x from the apex, that are similar to the base and scaled in area by (x/h)^2, giving V=∫[0,h](x/h)^2 A dx = ⅓Ah.

theorems.name: Pyramid/cone volume
theorems.statement: Any solid with a planar base of area A and apex at perpendicular distance h, whose cross-sections parallel to the base are similar copies of the base scaled linearly by x/h at distance x from the apex, has V=⅓Ah.
conditions: cross-sections are similar (same shape, linear scale factor) to the base
apex is a single point
h measured perpendicular to the base

formulas: V=⅓Ah (any cone/pyramid, curved or straight base)
A(x)=(x/h)^2·A for cross-section at distance x from apex
frustum volume = difference of two cone volumes

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Derive the ⅓Ah volume formula for a general cone/pyramid by setting up and evaluating the slicing integral.
question_archetypes.example: Show that a pyramid with base area A and height h has volume ⅓Ah.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks to justify or derive the ⅓Ah formula itself, not just plug into it — a 'prove that' or 'show that' style question.
method_plan: State that a cross-section at distance x from the apex is similar to the base with linear scale factor x/h
Write its area as (x/h)^2 A
Integrate from 0 to h and simplify
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct similarity scaling (x/h)^2
M1: correct integral setup
A1: correct evaluation to ⅓Ah

common_errors.description: Using linear scaling (x/h) instead of area scaling (x/h)^2
Errors integrating x^2 or simplifying the constant A/h^2
Not clearly stating why cross-sections are similar to the base

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Apply V=⅓Ah directly to a pyramid or cone with a given base shape and height.
question_archetypes.example: Find the volume of a pyramid with a square base of side 6 and height 10.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The base area and height are given (or easily computed) numbers and the solid is explicitly a cone/pyramid — a direct formula application, no integral needed.
method_plan: Compute the base area A
Apply V=⅓Ah
Simplify
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct base area
A1: correct application of V=⅓Ah

common_errors.description: Computing base area incorrectly (e.g. using perimeter instead of area)
Forgetting the factor of ⅓

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the volume of a frustum (a cone/pyramid with the top cut off) by slicing or by subtracting two cone volumes.
question_archetypes.example: Find the volume of a frustum of a cone with base radius R, top radius r, and height h.
question_archetypes.answer: V = (πh/3)(R^2+Rr+r^2), obtained by extending to the full cone, subtracting the small cone that was removed
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The solid is a truncated cone/pyramid (frustum) — direct slicing needs a linearly-varying radius/side function between the two given cross-sections.
method_plan: Set up the linear radius (or side) function interpolating between the two end cross-sections
Integrate A(x)=π[radius(x)]^2 (or polygon analogue) over the frustum's height, OR extend to the full cone and subtract the small cone's volume
Simplify to the closed form
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct linear interpolation for the varying radius/side
M1: correct integral or full-cone-minus-small-cone setup
A1: correct algebraic simplification
A1: correct final closed form

common_errors.description: Attempting to integrate the frustum directly with a complicated radius expression instead of subtracting two similar cones
Errors expanding [radius(x)]^2 for the linear interpolation
Forgetting the two sub-cones used in subtraction must be similar (same apex, same slant)

micro_skills.micro_skill: Arc length of a curve y=f(x) or x=g(y)
definitions: The arc length element is ds=√(1+(f'(x))^2) dx, obtained from the differential triangle (ds)^2=(dx)^2+(dy)^2; the arc length of y=f(x) on [a,b] is s=∫[a,b]√(1+(f'(x))^2) dx. A curve of finite arc length is called rectifiable.

theorems.name: Arc length formula
theorems.statement: If f' is continuous on [a,b], the arc length of y=f(x) from x=a to x=b is s=∫[a,b]√(1+(f'(x))^2)dx. If the curve is x=g(y), c≤y≤d, then s=∫[c,d]√(1+(g'(y))^2)dy.
conditions: f' (or g') continuous on the interval (piecewise continuous with finitely many breaks is enough in practice)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the arc length of y=f(x) on [a,b] where f' is a simple power function, leading to a substitution integral.
question_archetypes.example: Find the length of y=x^{3/2}·(2/3) from x=0 to x=3. [y'=√x, 1+(y')^2=1+x]
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The prompt gives an explicit y=f(x) and asks for arc length over a finite interval, and f' simplifies to something whose square is easy to add to 1.
method_plan: Differentiate f to get f'(x)
Form 1+(f'(x))^2 and simplify
Integrate √(1+(f'(x))^2), using substitution if needed
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct f'(x)
M1: correctly formed 1+(f')^2
A1: correct antiderivative
A1: correct evaluation

common_errors.description: Errors squaring f'(x) or simplifying 1+(f')^2
Forgetting the square root, integrating 1+(f')^2 directly
Not simplifying the final numeric answer

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the arc length of a curve whose 1+(f')^2 requires a nontrivial u-substitution to integrate.
question_archetypes.example: Find the length of y=x^{2/3} from x=1 to x=8. [y'=⅔x^{-1/3}]
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: 1+(f'(x))^2 simplifies to a fraction or a form that needs a substitution (often u = the expression under the root) rather than a direct power-rule antiderivative.
method_plan: Compute f'(x) and form 1+(f')^2, combining into a single fraction if needed
Choose a substitution u equal to the expression under the root (or its numerator)
Integrate in terms of u and convert limits
Evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct 1+(f')^2 simplified to a single expression
M1: valid substitution chosen and du computed correctly
A1: correct integration in u
A1: correct back-substitution/limit conversion and final value

common_errors.description: Errors combining terms into a single fraction under the root
Forgetting to convert the limits of integration to the new variable u
Attempting to integrate the un-simplified root directly instead of finding the substitution

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the arc length of a curve given as x=g(y) instead of y=f(x), integrating with respect to y.
question_archetypes.example: Find the length of x=⅓(y^2+2)^{3/2} from y=0 to y=2.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The curve is naturally given (or more easily solved) as x in terms of y, so the arc-length integral should be set up in dy, not dx.
method_plan: Differentiate x with respect to y to get g'(y)
Form 1+(g'(y))^2 and simplify
Integrate over the given y-interval
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct g'(y)
M1: correct simplification of 1+(g'(y))^2, ideally to a perfect square
A1: correct antiderivative
A1: correct evaluation

common_errors.description: Trying to invert to y=f(x) instead of working directly in y
Errors expanding y^2(y^2+2) or completing the simplification to a perfect square
Mixing dx and dy notation in the final integral

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize that a given arc-length integral (e.g. for an ellipse) does not have an elementary closed form, and express the answer as a named special integral / numerical value.
question_archetypes.example: Set up the arc length of the ellipse x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2=1 and explain why it cannot be evaluated in elementary terms.
question_archetypes.answer: s=4a∫[0,π/2]√(1-ε^2 sin^2 t)dt = 4aE(ε), the complete elliptic integral of the second kind — no elementary antiderivative exists
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The arc-length integrand, after correct setup, is a square root of a non-perfect-square trigonometric or algebraic expression that resists all standard integration techniques (a strong hint the answer is a named special function or numeric only).
method_plan: Parametrize the curve (e.g. x=a cos t, y=b sin t) and compute dx/dt, dy/dt
Form ds=√((dx/dt)^2+(dy/dt)^2)dt and simplify to standard elliptic-integral form
State that the result is the complete elliptic integral of the second kind, not elementary
Give the numeric value if requested, via a table or numerical approximation
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct parametrization and derivative computation
M1: correct simplified integrand matching elliptic-integral form
A1: correctly identifies/labels the non-elementary integral rather than attempting a bogus closed form
presentation: does not force an incorrect elementary antiderivative

common_errors.description: Spending excessive time trying to force an elementary antiderivative that does not exist
Not recognizing that some rectifiable curves have no elementary arc-length formula
Errors in the parametrization derivatives or in simplifying to the standard ε form

micro_skills.micro_skill: Surface area of a solid of revolution
definitions: Rotating the arc-length element ds about an axis at radius r sweeps a thin band of area dS=2πr ds; integrating gives the surface area of revolution S=∫2π(radius)ds.

theorems.name: Surface area of revolution
theorems.statement: For y=f(x) with f' continuous on [a,b], rotated about the x-axis, S=2π∫[a,b]|f(x)|√(1+(f'(x))^2)dx; rotated about the y-axis, S=2π∫[a,b]|x|√(1+(f'(x))^2)dx (analogous formulas for x=g(y)).
conditions: f' continuous on [a,b]
must use the true arc-length element ds, not dx, or the area is wrong (unlike the volume case)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the surface area generated by rotating y=f(x) about the x-axis.
question_archetypes.example: Rotate y=√x, 1≤x≤4, about the x-axis; find the surface area.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The curve is rotated about the x-axis and given as y=f(x); the prompt asks for surface area, not volume — look for 'surface area' or 'area of revolution' language.
method_plan: Compute f'(x) and form ds=√(1+(f'(x))^2)dx
Set up S=2π∫f(x)ds over the given interval
Simplify the integrand (combine into a single root) and integrate, using substitution if needed
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct ds
M1: correct S=2π∫f(x)ds setup
A1: correct simplification/substitution
A1: correct evaluation

common_errors.description: Using S=2π∫f(x)dx (a volume-style shortcut) instead of the true arc-length element ds
Errors combining f(x)·√(1+(f')^2) into a single square root before substituting
Dropping the factor of 2π

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the surface area generated by rotating a curve about the y-axis, using |x| as the radius.
question_archetypes.example: Rotate y=x^3, 0≤x≤1, about the y-axis; find the surface area.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Rotation is about the y-axis, so the radius of each band is |x|, not the curve's y-value — a common variant that catches students defaulting to the x-axis formula.
method_plan: Identify the radius as |x| since rotation is about the y-axis
Form ds and set up S=2π∫|x|ds
Substitute to integrate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct radius identified as x, not f(x)
M1: correct ds
A1: correct substitution/integration
A1: correct final value

common_errors.description: Using f(x) as the radius (correct for x-axis rotation) when the axis is actually the y-axis
Forgetting the substitution needed once x·√(1+9x^4) appears
Errors converting limits after substitution

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Derive the surface area of a sphere (or similar classical solid) using the surface-of-revolution formula and a key simplification.
question_archetypes.example: Rotate y=√(a^2-x^2), -a≤x≤a, about the x-axis; find the surface area (sphere of radius a).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The generating curve is a circular arc (or another classical curve) rotated about a coordinate axis, and a hidden algebraic simplification (using x^2+y^2=a^2) makes the y-factor cancel.
method_plan: Differentiate implicitly or explicitly to find dy/dx
Form ds and look for a simplification using the curve's defining equation
Substitute the simplified ds into S=2π∫y ds and integrate
Compare the result to the known closed-form surface area
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct derivative and ds
M1: correct algebraic simplification eliminating y from the integrand
A1: correct evaluation
A1: matches/checks against the known formula (e.g. 4πa^2)

common_errors.description: Not looking for the simplification and instead grinding through an unsimplified root
Sign or substitution errors using x^2+y^2=a^2
Not checking the final answer against the known closed-form result

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Identify and correct a surface-area setup that incorrectly used dx (or dy) alone instead of the true arc-length element ds.
question_archetypes.example: A student computes the surface area of y=x^2 rotated about the x-axis on [0,1] as S=2π∫[0,1]x^2 dx. Identify and correct the error.
question_archetypes.answer: Correct setup needs ds=√(1+4x^2)dx: S=2π∫[0,1]x^2√(1+4x^2)dx (not elementary in closed form without a substitution/table, illustrating why ds matters)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A surface-area computation is presented using a plain dx (or dy) factor with no square-root term — this is the volume-style shortcut mistakenly applied to a surface-area problem.
method_plan: Recall that surface-area bands must use the true slant width ds, not the flat width dx
Insert the correct ds=√(1+(f')^2)dx factor
Rewrite the corrected integral and note it may require different techniques than the flawed one
full_mark_rubric: M1: identifies the missing ds/arc-length factor as the error
M1: writes the corrected integral with the proper ds
A1: comments on why the flat-dx approximation is invalid for surface area (unlike for volume)

common_errors.description: Believing the flat cylindrical-band approximation (valid for volume) is also valid for surface area
Inserting ds but forgetting to also keep the correct radius factor (f(x) or x)
Not explaining why the error matters (the discrepancy does not vanish in the limit for slanted curves)

micro_skills.subtopic: Mass, Moments, and Centre of Mass
micro_skills.micro_skill: Mass, moment, and centre of mass of a 1-D wire/rod
definitions: For a rod/wire on [a,b] with continuous line density δ(x), the mass is m=∫[a,b]δ(x)dx and the moment about x=0 is M_{x=0}=∫[a,b]xδ(x)dx; the centre of mass is x̄=M_{x=0}/m.

theorems.name: Centre of mass (1-D)
theorems.statement: For a continuum on [a,b] with line density δ(x), m=∫[a,b]δ(x)dx, M_{x=0}=∫[a,b]xδ(x)dx, and x̄=M_{x=0}/m.
conditions: δ continuous (or piecewise continuous) on [a,b]

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the mass, moment, and centre of mass of a wire on [0,L] with a given line density function.
question_archetypes.example: A wire on [0,L] has density δ(x)=kx. Find m, M_{x=0}, and x̄.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A 1-D rod/wire is described with an explicit density function of position and the question asks for mass and/or centre of mass — a direct application of the two integrals and their ratio.
method_plan: Integrate δ(x) over the wire to get m
Integrate xδ(x) to get M_{x=0}
Divide to get x̄
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct mass integral and evaluation
M1: correct moment integral and evaluation
A1: correct division to get x̄
A1: sensible final answer (x̄ within [0,L])

common_errors.description: Forgetting to divide the moment by the mass (reporting M instead of x̄)
Errors integrating kx or kx^2
Not sanity-checking that x̄ lies within the physical extent of the wire

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the mass and centre of mass of a rod whose density is defined piecewise (or as a sum of two densities).
question_archetypes.example: A rod on [0,4] has δ(x)=2 for 0≤x<2 and δ(x)=x for 2≤x≤4. Find m and x̄.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The density function is given in separate pieces over sub-intervals, requiring the mass and moment integrals to be split and summed.
method_plan: Split the mass and moment integrals at the breakpoint(s)
Evaluate each piece separately
Sum the pieces before dividing to find x̄
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly split integrals at the breakpoint
A1: correct evaluation of each piece
A1: correct sum and final x̄

common_errors.description: Forgetting to split the integral at the density's breakpoint
Arithmetic errors combining the pieces
Not clearly labelling which piece corresponds to which sub-interval

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the moment of a rod about a point other than x=0, and relate it to the moment about x=0.
question_archetypes.example: For the wire δ(x)=kx on [0,L], find the moment about the point x=L (the right end).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks for a moment (or balance point/torque) about a specified pivot other than the origin — requires shifting the moment arm to (x-pivot).
method_plan: Write the moment arm as (x - pivot) instead of x
Integrate (x-pivot)δ(x) over the rod
Optionally relate the result to M_{x=0} and m via M_{pivot}=M_{x=0}-pivot·m
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct moment-arm expression (x-pivot)
M1: correct integral setup
A1: correct evaluation
A1: correct sign/interpretation of the result

common_errors.description: Using x as the moment arm instead of (x-pivot)
Sign errors expanding (x-pivot)δ(x)
Not interpreting a negative moment as indicating which side of the pivot the mass concentrates on

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine whether an infinite (unbounded) wire has finite total mass, using an improper integral.
question_archetypes.example: A wire on [1,∞) has density δ(x)=1/x^2. Find its total mass, if finite.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The wire/rod extends to infinity, so the mass integral is improper and convergence must be checked before (or while) computing the mass.
method_plan: Set up the mass integral with the infinite limit
Rewrite as a limit of a proper integral over [1,R]
Evaluate and take the limit, stating convergence or divergence
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly rewrote as a limit
A1: correct antiderivative
A1: correct limit evaluation and convergence conclusion

common_errors.description: Plugging in ∞ directly rather than taking a limit
Assuming an infinite wire must always have infinite mass
Not checking convergence before attempting to also compute x̄ (which may diverge even if m converges)

micro_skills.subtopic: Mass, Moments, and Centre of Mass
micro_skills.micro_skill: Mass and centre of mass of a planar plate
definitions: For a plate occupying a≤x≤b, 0≤y≤f(x) with density ρ(x) depending only on x, m=∫[a,b]ρ(x)f(x)dx, M_{x=0}=∫[a,b]xρ(x)f(x)dx, M_{y=0}=½∫[a,b]ρ(x)[f(x)]^2dx (the ½ arises because a vertical strip's own centre of mass sits at its midpoint height ½f(x)), and x̄=M_{x=0}/m, ȳ=M_{y=0}/m.

theorems.name: Moments of a plate
theorems.statement: For a≤x≤b, 0≤y≤f(x) with density ρ(x): m=∫ρ(x)f(x)dx, M_{x=0}=∫xρ(x)f(x)dx, M_{y=0}=½∫ρ(x)[f(x)]^2dx.
conditions: ρ depends only on x (constant across each vertical strip)
f continuous and nonnegative on [a,b]

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the mass and centre of mass of a plate under y=f(x) with a given density ρ(x).
question_archetypes.example: A plate occupies 0≤x≤2, 0≤y≤x^2 with density ρ(x)=3. Find m, x̄, ȳ.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A 2-D plate bounded by y=f(x) is described with a density depending only on x, and both x̄ and ȳ are requested.
method_plan: Set up and evaluate m=∫ρ(x)f(x)dx
Set up and evaluate M_{x=0}=∫xρ(x)f(x)dx for x̄
Set up and evaluate M_{y=0}=½∫ρ(x)[f(x)]^2dx for ȳ
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct mass integral
M1: correct M_{x=0} integral
A1: correct M_{y=0} integral including the ½ factor
A1: correct x̄ and ȳ

common_errors.description: Using f(x) instead of ½[f(x)]^2 in M_{y=0} (forgetting the strip's own centroid height)
Errors integrating powers of x
Dividing the wrong moment by m (swapping x̄ and ȳ)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the centre of mass of a plate between two curves f(x) (upper) and g(x) (lower), with density ρ(x).
question_archetypes.example: Plate between y=√x (upper) and y=x^2 (lower), 0≤x≤1, density ρ(x)=1+x. Find m, x̄, ȳ.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The plate lies between two curves (not simply under one curve down to y=0), so both the height (upper−lower) and the M_{y=0} formula (upper²−lower²) must account for both boundaries.
method_plan: Identify upper and lower boundary functions
Write height=upper−lower for m and M_{x=0}
Use M_{y=0}=½∫ρ(x)([upper]^2-[lower]^2)dx (not just ½[upper]^2)
Evaluate and divide for x̄, ȳ
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct height=upper−lower used in m and M_{x=0}
M1: correct M_{y=0}=½∫ρ([upper]^2-[lower]^2)dx
A1: correct evaluation of all integrals
A1: correct final x̄, ȳ

common_errors.description: Using ½[upper]^2 alone for M_{y=0}, ignoring the lower boundary's contribution
Using upper−lower in m but forgetting the same adjustment is needed (squared form) in M_{y=0}
Errors expanding or simplifying (1+x)(√x-x^2) or similar products

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize that a plate whose density depends on y (not just x) cannot be handled by the standard vertical-strip formulas without further reformulation.
question_archetypes.example: A plate under y=f(x), 0≤x≤b, has density ρ(x,y)=y (depends on the height within the strip, not just x). Explain why m=∫ρ(x)f(x)dx does not directly apply, and describe what must change.
question_archetypes.answer: Since density varies within each vertical strip, a single-variable formula ρ(x)·(strip length) is invalid; the strip's mass requires integrating ρ over y first (∫[0,f(x)]y dy=½f(x)^2 if ρ=y), or the problem must be handled with a double integral in general
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The stated density is a function of both x and y (or of y alone), so a vertical strip no longer has uniform density along its height — the single-integral plate formulas silently assume ρ=ρ(x) only.
method_plan: Check whether the given density depends on y as well as x
If so, note the vertical-strip mass requires an inner integration over y within the strip before integrating over x
Set up the (possibly double) integral, or note this generally requires double-integral methods beyond a single-variable strip
full_mark_rubric: M1: recognizes the density genuinely varies within a vertical strip
M1: correctly sets up the inner y-integral for the strip's mass (when tractable in closed form)
A1: correctly notes the limitation of the single-integral plate formulas
presentation: clear explanation, not just a formula recited from memory

common_errors.description: Applying m=∫ρ(x)f(x)dx unchanged even though ρ depends on y
Not recognizing this is a double-integral setup in disguise, outside the single-integral toolkit
Giving a numeric answer without acknowledging the extra integration needed within each strip

micro_skills.subtopic: Mass, Moments, and Centre of Mass
micro_skills.micro_skill: Mass and centre of mass of a 3-D solid via slicing
definitions: For a solid of revolution or radially symmetric solid, mass is found by combining a volume element (disk, shell, or spherical shell) with a density function, dm=ρ dV, then m=∫dm and, e.g., M_{z=0}=∫zρ dV for the moment about a plane, with z̄=M_{z=0}/m.

theorems.name: Mass via slicing
theorems.statement: If a solid's volume element at position x (or radius r) is dV(x) and density is ρ(x), then m=∫ρ(x)dV(x) and the moment about a reference plane is M=∫(position)·ρ(x)dV(x), giving the centre-of-mass coordinate as M/m.
conditions: density depends only on the slicing variable (x, z, or r) so it is constant across each volume element

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the mass and centre of mass of a solid of revolution with depth-dependent density, using disk slices.
question_archetypes.example: A solid hemisphere of radius R has density ρ0·z at height z above its base. Find m and z̄.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A solid of revolution (sphere, cone, etc.) has a density given as an explicit function of the slicing coordinate (e.g. height z) — combine the disk volume element with that density.
method_plan: Find the disk's radius and volume element dV(z) as in Section 7.1
Multiply by the given density ρ(z) to get dm
Integrate dm for mass and z·dm for the moment
Divide for z̄
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct dV(z) from the disk method
M1: correct dm=ρ(z)dV
A1: correct mass and moment integrals evaluated
A1: correct z̄

common_errors.description: Reusing the constant-density disk-volume formula without multiplying by ρ(z)
Errors expanding ρ0z(R^2-z^2)
Confusing the centroid (z=R·something with ρ=1) with the density-weighted centre of mass

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the mass of a spherically symmetric solid with a radius-dependent density, using spherical shell volume elements.
question_archetypes.example: A planet of radius R has density ρ(r)=ρ0/(1+r^2). Find its total mass.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The solid is described as radially symmetric (a ball/planet) with density depending only on the distance r from the centre — this calls for spherical shell elements dV=4πr^2dr, not disks.
method_plan: Recall the spherical shell volume element dV=4πr^2dr
Multiply by ρ(r) to form dm
Integrate from r=0 to R, using algebraic manipulation (e.g. splitting a fraction) if the integrand isn't immediately elementary
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct shell volume element 4πr^2dr
M1: correct dm=ρ(r)·4πr^2dr set up
A1: correct algebraic manipulation of the integrand (e.g. r^2/(1+r^2)=1-1/(1+r^2))
A1: correct evaluation including arctan

common_errors.description: Using a disk/washer element (2-D cross-section logic) instead of the spherical shell element 4πr^2dr for a 3-D radially symmetric solid
Failing to rewrite r^2/(1+r^2) in an integrable form
Forgetting the factor of 4π from the shell surface area

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the mass of a solid of revolution using cylindrical shells combined with a radius-dependent density.
question_archetypes.example: A cylindrical solid of radius R and height h is formed by rotating [0,R]×[0,h] about its axis, with density ρ(r)=k/r (r=distance from axis, r>0). Find the mass using shells.
question_archetypes.answer: dV=2πrh dr (shell of radius r, height h); dm=(k/r)(2πrh)dr=2πkh dr; m=∫[ε,R]2πkh dr=2πkh(R-ε) (or note the density is singular at r=0, requiring care/an improper-integral check as ε→0)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Density is naturally given as a function of the radial distance from an axis in a solid formed by rotation — using cylindrical shells (dV=2πr·height·dr) makes the density substitution direct.
method_plan: Recall the shell volume element dV=2π(radius)(height)dr for this axis-symmetric solid
Substitute the density ρ(r) to form dm
Integrate over the radius, checking for improper behaviour if ρ(r) blows up at r=0
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct shell element with radius and height correctly identified
M1: correct dm=ρ(r)dV
A1: correct integration, including any necessary limit/improper-integral treatment
A1: correct final mass or correct conclusion about divergence

common_errors.description: Not noticing the density is singular at the axis and blindly integrating from r=0 without checking convergence
Using disks instead of shells when the density is naturally a function of radial distance
Not simplifying ρ(r)·2πr before integrating, missing an easy cancellation

micro_skills.micro_skill: Centroid of a standard plane region (constant density)
definitions: When density is constant it cancels out of the x̄, ȳ formulas, leaving a point depending only on the region's shape, called the centroid. For a≤x≤b, 0≤y≤f(x): A=∫f(x)dx, M_{x=0}=∫xf(x)dx, M_{y=0}=½∫[f(x)]^2dx, x̄=M_{x=0}/A, ȳ=M_{y=0}/A.

theorems.name: Centroid of a plane region
theorems.statement: For the region a≤x≤b, 0≤y≤f(x): A=∫[a,b]f(x)dx, x̄=(1/A)∫[a,b]xf(x)dx, ȳ=(1/A)·½∫[a,b][f(x)]^2dx.
conditions: f continuous and nonnegative on [a,b]
density constant (so it cancels)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the centroid of the region under a single curve y=f(x) on [a,b].
question_archetypes.example: Find the centroid of the region bounded by y=4-x^2 and y=0, -2≤x≤2.
question_archetypes.answer: By symmetry x̄=0; A=32/3; M_{y=0}=∫0^2(16-8x^2+x^4)dx=256/15 (doubling the even integrand); ȳ=8/5. Centroid (0, 8/5).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A single curve and the x-axis bound a region and the question asks directly for the centroid (x̄, ȳ) — the standard, unadorned centroid formula applies.
method_plan: Use symmetry to simplify x̄ if the region is symmetric
Compute A=∫f(x)dx
Compute M_{y=0}=½∫[f(x)]^2dx and divide by A for ȳ
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct area A
M1: correct M_{y=0} with the ½ factor
A1: correct ȳ
A1: correct x̄ (via symmetry or direct integration)

Errors expanding [f(x)]^2

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the centroid of a region bounded between two curves f(x) (upper) and g(x) (lower).
question_archetypes.example: Find the centroid of the region between y=√x and y=x^2, 0≤x≤1.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The region is bounded above and below by two distinct curves — both A and M_{y=0} must use (upper−lower) and ([upper]^2−[lower]^2) respectively.
method_plan: Find intersection points for limits
Compute A=∫(upper−lower)dx and M_{x=0}=∫x(upper−lower)dx
Compute M_{y=0}=½∫([upper]^2−[lower]^2)dx
Divide for x̄, ȳ
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct limits from intersections
M1: correct A and M_{x=0} using (upper−lower)
A1: correct M_{y=0} using squared difference
A1: correct final x̄, ȳ

Errors finding intersection points
Inconsistent upper/lower assignment between the A and M_{y=0} computations

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use symmetry to reduce the work of finding a centroid, without setting up a full integral for the symmetric coordinate.
question_archetypes.example: Find the centroid of a semicircular region of radius a (flat side on the x-axis, centred at the origin).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The region has an obvious axis of symmetry — recognizing it immediately gives one coordinate of the centroid for free, without integration.
method_plan: Identify the axis of symmetry and set the corresponding centroid coordinate to the symmetry axis value directly
Compute only the remaining, non-trivial coordinate via integration
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly uses symmetry to state one coordinate immediately
M1: correct area
A1: correct moment integral for the remaining coordinate
A1: correct final centroid

common_errors.description: Computing the symmetric coordinate by full integration anyway, wasting time
Errors evaluating the semicircle moment integral
Misidentifying the axis of symmetry (e.g. assuming symmetry about the wrong line)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Identify and correct an error in a centroid computation that omitted the ½ factor needed for M_{y=0} (a common exam mistake).
question_archetypes.example: A student computes the centroid of y=x^2, 0≤x≤2, y=0, using M_{y=0}=∫[0,2]x^4dx instead of ½∫[0,2]x^4dx. Identify the error and give the corrected ȳ.
question_archetypes.answer: Correct M_{y=0}=½∫[0,2]x^4dx=16/5; with A=8/3, ȳ=(16/5)/(8/3)=6/5 (the flawed computation would give double this)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A worked centroid solution is presented for critique, and the moment about y=0 for a region (not a curve) is computed without the ½ factor that accounts for each strip's own midpoint height.
method_plan: Recall that a vertical strip's centre of mass is at its midpoint height ½f(x), not at f(x)
Insert the missing ½ factor into M_{y=0}
Recompute ȳ with the corrected moment
full_mark_rubric: M1: identifies the missing ½ factor as the error
A1: correct recomputed M_{y=0}
A1: correct recomputed ȳ

common_errors.description: Omitting the ½ factor in M_{y=0}=½∫[f(x)]^2dx for a 2-D region
Not understanding why the ½ factor arises (each strip's own centroid is at its midpoint, not its top)
Not clearly recomputing both M_{y=0} and the resulting ȳ after finding the error

micro_skills.micro_skill: Centroid of a triangle via vertex averaging
definitions: The centroid of a triangle is the intersection of its three medians, and equals the average of its three vertices' coordinates: (x̄,ȳ)=((x1+x2+x3)/3, (y1+y2+y3)/3).

theorems.name: Centroid of a triangle
theorems.statement: For a triangle with vertices (x1,y1), (x2,y2), (x3,y3), the centroid is ((x1+x2+x3)/3, (y1+y2+y3)/3), and it lies at the common intersection point of the three medians (each median divides it 2:1 from vertex to midpoint of the opposite side).
conditions: applies to any triangle (not restricted to right or isosceles triangles)

formulas: each median is divided 2:1 by the centroid, measured from the vertex

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the centroid of a triangle given its three vertex coordinates.
question_archetypes.example: Find the centroid of the triangle with vertices (0,0), (6,0), (0,9).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Three explicit vertex coordinates are given and the centroid is requested — a direct average, no integration needed.
method_plan: Average the three x-coordinates for x̄
Average the three y-coordinates for ȳ
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct averaging formula applied
A1: correct x̄ and ȳ

common_errors.description: Arithmetic slip averaging the coordinates
Confusing the centroid with the circumcentre or incentre (different triangle centers)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Verify that the centroid found by vertex-averaging lies on a specific median and divides it in ratio 2:1.
question_archetypes.example: For the triangle (0,0), (6,0), (0,9), verify the centroid (2,3) lies on the median from (0,0) to the midpoint of the opposite side, and divides it 2:1.
question_archetypes.answer: Midpoint of side from (6,0) to (0,9) is (3, 4.5). The median from (0,0) to (3,4.5) is parametrized (3t,4.5t); at t=2/3 this gives (2,3) — matches the centroid, confirming the 2:1 division.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem explicitly asks to confirm/derive the median property rather than just compute the centroid — a justification-style question.
method_plan: Find the midpoint of one side
Parametrize the median from the opposite vertex to that midpoint
Show the centroid corresponds to parameter t=2/3 along that median (2:1 split)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct midpoint computed
M1: correct parametrization of the median
A1: correctly shows t=2/3 lands on the centroid
presentation: clear conclusion about the 2:1 ratio

common_errors.description: Errors finding the midpoint of a side
Parametrizing the median in the wrong direction (from midpoint to vertex vs. vertex to midpoint), flipping the ratio
Not connecting the parameter value to the 2:1 ratio interpretation

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the centroid of a general polygon by decomposing it into triangles and combining moments.
question_archetypes.example: Find the centroid of the quadrilateral with vertices (0,0), (4,0), (5,3), (1,4).
question_archetypes.answer: Split into triangles (0,0)-(4,0)-(5,3) and (0,0)-(5,3)-(1,4); compute each triangle's area and centroid (vertex average), then combine via A_total·x̄=ΣA_i x̄_i (and similarly for ȳ)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The shape is not a single triangle (a general polygon), so the vertex-average shortcut doesn't apply directly to the whole shape — it must first be triangulated.
method_plan: Split the polygon into non-overlapping triangles
Find each triangle's area and centroid (vertex average)
Combine using the composite-region formula ΣA_i x̄_i / ΣA_i (and similarly for ȳ)
full_mark_rubric: M1: valid triangulation with no overlaps/gaps
M1: correct area and centroid for each triangle
A1: correct composite formula applied
A1: correct final centroid

common_errors.description: Trying to average all four vertices directly (only valid for a triangle, not a general quadrilateral)
Overlapping or gapped triangulation, double-counting or missing area
Errors computing individual triangle areas (e.g. via the shoelace formula or ½ base×height)

micro_skills.micro_skill: Centroid of a composite region (sum/difference of pieces)
definitions: If a region is a union of nonoverlapping pieces (or a shape with a piece removed), moments add (or subtract): M_{x=0}=ΣA_i x̄_i and M_{y=0}=ΣA_i ȳ_i, so the composite centroid is x̄=ΣA_i x̄_i/ΣA_i (and analogously for ȳ) — note it is the moments, not the centroids themselves, that add.

theorems.name: Composite region centroid
theorems.statement: If a region R is partitioned into nonoverlapping pieces R_i with areas A_i and centroids (x̄_i,ȳ_i), then the centroid of R is x̄=(ΣA_ix̄_i)/(ΣA_i), ȳ=(ΣA_iȳ_i)/(ΣA_i). A removed 'hole' piece is included with a negative area.
conditions: pieces do not overlap
a subtracted hole must lie entirely inside the outer region

formulas: hole/subtracted piece contributes with negative A_i

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the centroid of a shape formed by joining two simple shapes (e.g. a rectangle and a triangle).
question_archetypes.example: An L-shaped region is a 4×2 rectangle with a 2×2 square attached on top of one end. Find the centroid.
question_archetypes.answer: Split into rectangle (area 8, centroid (2,1)) and square (area 4, centroid (1,3)); x̄=(8·2+4·1)/12=5/3, ȳ=(8·1+4·3)/12=5/3
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The region is visibly a union of two or more standard shapes (rectangles, triangles, semicircles) joined along an edge — decompose and combine via the composite formula.
method_plan: Split the region into standard shapes with known area and centroid
List each piece's area and centroid coordinates
Apply x̄=ΣA_ix̄_i/ΣA_i and ȳ=ΣA_iȳ_i/ΣA_i
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct decomposition into standard pieces
M1: correct area and centroid for each piece
A1: correct weighted-average formula applied
A1: correct final x̄, ȳ

common_errors.description: Averaging the centroids directly (unweighted) instead of weighting by each piece's area
Placing piece centroids in the wrong local coordinate frame (forgetting to reference the same global origin)
Arithmetic errors in the weighted sum

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the centroid of a region with a piece (hole) removed, treating the hole as a negative area.
question_archetypes.example: A 6×6 square (centroid (3,3), area 36) has a 2×2 square hole removed from a corner (centred at (1,1), area 4). Find the centroid of the remaining region.
question_archetypes.answer: x̄=(36·3-4·1)/(36-4)=104/32=13/4; ȳ=13/4 by the same computation (symmetry of this particular example)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The shape is described as a standard region with a smaller piece cut out (a hole, notch, or bore) — the removed piece's area and moment must be subtracted, not ignored.
method_plan: Find the area and centroid of the full outer shape
Find the area and centroid of the removed piece
Subtract the hole's area and moment from the outer shape's, then divide by the net area
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct outer shape area/centroid
M1: correct hole area/centroid
A1: correctly subtracts (not adds) the hole's contribution
A1: correct final centroid using the net area in the denominator

common_errors.description: Adding the hole's moment instead of subtracting it
Dividing by the outer area instead of the net (outer − hole) area
Errors locating the hole's centroid relative to the global coordinate system

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the centroid of a composite region built from a mix of shapes including at least one via direct integration (not a standard formula).
question_archetypes.example: A region consists of a semicircle of radius a (flat side up, on top of a rectangle of width 2a and height h). Find the composite centroid.
question_archetypes.answer: Semicircle: area πa^2/2, centroid at height h+4a/(3π) above the base (using the known semicircle centroid distance from its flat edge); rectangle: area 2ah, centroid at height h/2. Combine via ȳ=(A1ȳ1+A2ȳ2)/(A1+A2); x̄=a by symmetry throughout.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: One or more pieces of the composite shape do not have an 'obvious' centroid (like a semicircle) and require recalling or re-deriving a standard sub-result before combining.
method_plan: Identify each piece and recall (or derive) its individual centroid, translating to the shared coordinate system
Carefully track each piece's centroid relative to the common origin, not its own local origin
Combine via the weighted composite formula
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct individual centroid for the non-trivial piece (e.g. semicircle), correctly translated to the global frame
M1: correct area/centroid for the remaining piece(s)
A1: correct weighted combination
A1: correct final centroid coordinates

common_errors.description: Using a sub-shape's centroid measured from its own local origin instead of translating to the shared coordinate system
Forgetting a known standard centroid result (e.g. semicircle's ȳ=4a/(3π) from its flat edge) and mis-deriving it
Errors adding the translation offset to the local centroid value

micro_skills.micro_skill: Pappus's Theorem for volumes and surface areas of revolution
definitions: Pappus's Theorem: (a) if a plane region R lies entirely on one side of a line L in its plane and is rotated about L, the volume generated is V=2πr̄A, where A is R's area and r̄ is the distance from R's centroid to L; (b) if a plane curve C lies on one side of L and is rotated about L, the surface area generated is S=2πr̄s, where s is C's arc length and r̄ is the distance from C's centroid to L.

theorems.name: Pappus's Theorem
theorems.statement: V=2π r̄ A (volume of revolution of a region) and S=2π r̄ s (surface area of revolution of a curve), where r̄ is the distance from the relevant centroid to the axis L.
conditions: the region/curve lies entirely on one side of L (does not cross it)
L lies in the same plane as the region/curve

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use Pappus's Theorem to find a volume of revolution given the region's area and centroid.
question_archetypes.example: The disk (x-5)^2+y^2≤4 is rotated about the y-axis. Find the resulting volume.
question_archetypes.answer: Centroid distance r̄=5, area A=4π; V=2π(5)(4π)=40π^2
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The area and centroid of the rotated region are already known (or trivially computable, as for a disk), and only the volume is requested — Pappus gives it in one step, no integral needed.
method_plan: Identify the region's area A
Identify the distance r̄ from the region's centroid to the axis of rotation
Apply V=2πr̄A
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct area A
M1: correct r̄ (distance from centroid to axis, not from an edge)
A1: correct application of V=2πr̄A

common_errors.description: Using the distance from the near or far edge of the region instead of from its centroid
Forgetting the factor of 2π
Attempting a full disk/washer/shell integral instead of recognizing Pappus applies directly

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use Pappus's Theorem in reverse — recover an unknown centroid distance from a known volume or surface area.
question_archetypes.example: Rotating a semicircular region of radius a about its diameter gives a sphere of volume 4πa^3/3. Use Pappus to find the centroid's distance ȳ from the diameter.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The volume (or surface area) of the solid generated is already known from another source (a standard formula), and the centroid distance is the unknown to be solved for — Pappus used 'backwards'.
method_plan: Identify the known volume (or surface area) and the region's (or curve's) area (or arc length)
Set up V=2πr̄A (or S=2πr̄s) with r̄ as the unknown
Solve algebraically for r̄
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct known volume/area/arc-length values identified
M1: correct Pappus equation set up with r̄ as unknown
A1: correct algebraic solution for r̄
A1: sanity-check that r̄ is a plausible distance for the shape

common_errors.description: Confusing which of A or s (region area vs. curve length) pairs with which of V or S
Errors isolating r̄ algebraically
Not recognizing this as a Pappus problem and instead attempting to re-derive the centroid via a fresh integral

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use Pappus's Theorem to find a surface area of revolution from a curve's arc length and centroid.
question_archetypes.example: The boundary circle (radius a) of a disk centred at (b,0), b>a, is rotated about the y-axis. Find the surface area of the resulting torus.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks for a surface area generated by rotating a curve (not the enclosed region) — matching s (arc length) and r̄ (curve's centroid distance) in the S=2πr̄s formula, not the volume version.
method_plan: Identify that only the boundary curve (not the filled region) is being rotated
Find its arc length s and the distance r̄ from its centroid to the axis
Apply S=2πr̄s
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly distinguishes curve (S formula) from region (V formula)
M1: correct arc length s
A1: correct r̄
A1: correct application of S=2πr̄s

common_errors.description: Using the region's area/centroid (V formula) when the problem is actually about the boundary curve (S formula)
Errors computing the curve's arc length
Not stating explicitly which Pappus formula (volume or surface) is being used and why

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize a situation where Pappus's Theorem cannot be applied directly because the axis of rotation passes through the region/curve, and explain the necessary workaround.
question_archetypes.example: A region straddles the x-axis (part above, part below) and is rotated about the x-axis. Can Pappus's Theorem be applied directly? If not, how should the volume be found?
question_archetypes.answer: No — Pappus requires the region to lie entirely on one side of the axis; since it crosses, split the region into the parts above and below the axis, apply Pappus (or direct integration) to each separately, and combine appropriately (noting rotation of the below-axis part sweeps the same solid as its mirror image above)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The region or curve is explicitly described as crossing, straddling, or touching both sides of the axis of rotation — a direct disqualifier for applying Pappus's Theorem as stated.
method_plan: Check whether the region/curve lies entirely on one side of the axis
If it crosses, split into pieces that each lie on one side
Apply Pappus (or direct integration) to each piece and combine, being careful not to double count overlapping swept volume
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies that Pappus's hypothesis is violated
M1: valid splitting strategy proposed
A1: correct treatment of the split pieces avoiding double-counting
presentation: clear justification referencing the theorem's 'one side of L' condition

common_errors.description: Applying Pappus's Theorem directly to a region that crosses the axis, getting a nonsensical or wrong volume
Not realizing the pieces on each side may sweep out overlapping (not additive) volume, requiring care
Not explicitly citing the 'lies entirely on one side of L' hypothesis as the reason the direct formula fails

micro_skills.micro_skill: Centroid of a curve (arc), as distinct from a region's centroid
definitions: The centroid of a plane curve C (as opposed to the region it may enclose) is found using arc length in place of area: x̄=(1/s)∫x ds, ȳ=(1/s)∫y ds, where s=∫ds is the total arc length. This is generally a different point from the centroid of the region the curve bounds, and need not lie on the curve itself.

theorems.name: Centroid of a curve
theorems.statement: For a curve C with arc length s, x̄=(1/s)∫_C x ds, ȳ=(1/s)∫_C y ds.
conditions: ds is the true arc-length element
curve is rectifiable (finite s)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the centroid of a semicircular arc (curve only, not the enclosed region) using arc length.
question_archetypes.example: Find the centroid of the semicircular arc y=√(a^2-x^2), -a≤x≤a.
question_archetypes.answer: By symmetry x̄=0. Using ds=a dx/√(a^2-x^2): M=∫[-a,a]y ds=∫[-a,a]a dx=2a^2; s=πa; ȳ=2a^2/(πa)=2a/π
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem explicitly asks for the centroid of a curve/arc/wire (as opposed to a filled region or plate) — a signal to integrate with ds, not dx or dy, and to divide by arc length s, not area.
method_plan: Compute the arc-length element ds
Set up M=∫y ds (or x ds) and s=∫ds
Divide M by s to get the centroid coordinate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct ds
M1: correct moment integral ∫y ds
A1: correct arc length s
A1: correct final centroid coordinate = moment/s

common_errors.description: Using the region's centroid formula (ȳ=½∫y^2dx / area) instead of the curve's (ȳ=∫y ds / s)
Errors simplifying ds=a dx/√(a^2-x^2) or evaluating the resulting integral
Dividing by area instead of arc length s

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Explicitly compare and contrast the centroid of a curve with the centroid of the region it bounds, showing they differ.
question_archetypes.example: Compare the centroid of the semicircular arc y=√(a^2-x^2) (ȳ=2a/π) with the centroid of the semicircular region it bounds (ȳ=4a/(3π)). Explain why they differ.
question_archetypes.answer: 2a/π ≈ 0.637a vs 4a/(3π) ≈ 0.424a — different points; the curve's centroid weights each point equally by arc length (uniform wire), while the region's centroid weights by the strip's extent (more 'mass' concentrated toward the wider parts of the disk), pulling the region's centroid closer to the flat base.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks explicitly for a comparison, a 'why do these differ' explanation, or presents two answers and asks which is correct for 'centroid of the boundary' vs. 'centroid of the region'.
method_plan: Compute (or recall) both centroids using their respective formulas
Compare the numeric values
Explain the conceptual reason for the difference (uniform arc-length weighting vs. area/strip weighting)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct curve centroid
M1: correct region centroid
A1: correct numeric comparison
A1: clear conceptual explanation of why the two differ

common_errors.description: Assuming a curve and the region it bounds must share the same centroid
Giving both numeric answers without explaining the underlying reason they differ
Errors in either individual centroid computation

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use the centroid of a curve together with Pappus's Theorem to compute (or check) a surface area of revolution.
question_archetypes.example: Using the semicircular arc's centroid ȳ=2a/π (distance from the diameter), verify via Pappus that rotating the arc about the diameter gives the sphere's surface area 4πa^2.
question_archetypes.answer: s=πa (arc length), r̄=2a/π; S=2π r̄ s=2π(2a/π)(πa)=4πa^2, matching the known sphere surface area — confirms the arc centroid.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem links the curve's centroid to a known solid's surface area via Pappus, either to verify the centroid or to compute the surface area using it — a cross-check or 'confirm using Pappus' style question.
method_plan: Recall/compute the arc's centroid distance r̄ and its arc length s
Apply S=2πr̄s
Compare to the known/expected surface area as a consistency check
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct r̄ and s used
M1: correct application of S=2πr̄s
A1: correct final surface area matching the expected value
A1: explicit statement that this confirms the arc centroid (or vice versa)

common_errors.description: Using the region's centroid/area instead of the curve's centroid/arc-length in the Pappus surface formula
Errors in the multiplication or in recalling s=πa for a semicircular arc
Not using the known sphere surface area as an independent check on the computed centroid

micro_skills.micro_skill: Hydrostatic pressure and force on a submerged plate
definitions: Pressure at depth h in a fluid of density ρ is p=ρgh (acting equally in all directions). For a submerged vertical plate, slicing into horizontal strips of width w(h) at depth h gives a force element dF=ρgh·w(h)dh, and total force F=∫ρgh w(h)dh.

theorems.name: Hydrostatic force
theorems.statement: For a vertical plate submerged with a horizontal strip of width w(h) at depth h, F=∫ρgh·w(h)dh over the submerged depth range. For a plate inclined at angle θ to the vertical, an extra factor secθ multiplies the strip's width (measuring along the slanted face).
conditions: h measured as vertical depth below the fluid surface
w(h) is the horizontal (or slant-corrected) width of the plate at depth h

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the hydrostatic force on a vertical rectangular plate submerged with its top edge at (or below) the fluid surface.
question_archetypes.example: A vertical dam gate is a rectangle 6 m wide, 4 m tall, top edge at the water surface. Find the total hydrostatic force (ρg=9800 N/m^3).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The submerged shape is a simple rectangle with constant width, and the top is at (or the depth range is clearly given from) the surface — the most direct hydrostatic setup.
method_plan: Identify the constant width w and the depth range
Set up F=ρg w∫h dh over that depth range
Evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct width and depth limits
M1: correct integral setup with ρg included
A1: correct evaluation
A1: correct units/final numeric answer
