common_errors.description: Using p=ρgh only (pressure) instead of integrating to get total force
Forgetting to multiply by the constant width w before integrating
Omitting units or the ρg constant in the final numeric answer

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the hydrostatic force on a submerged plate whose width varies with depth according to a curved boundary (e.g. circular or parabolic).
question_archetypes.example: A vertical semicircular plate of radius R (curved edge down) is submerged full to the top. Find the force.
question_archetypes.answer: Width at depth h is 2√(R^2-h^2); F=∫[0,R]ρgh·2√(R^2-h^2)dh, u=R^2-h^2 ⇒ F=(2/3)ρgR^3
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The plate's cross-section is a non-rectangular shape (circle, semicircle, triangle, trapezoid) so the strip width w(h) must be derived from the shape's boundary curve/equation before integrating.
method_plan: Express the strip width w(h) as a function of depth using the plate's boundary equation
Set up F=∫ρgh w(h)dh
Integrate, using substitution if the width involves a square root
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct w(h) derived from the boundary shape
M1: correct integral setup
A1: correct substitution/integration
A1: correct final force

common_errors.description: Errors deriving w(h) from the circle/shape equation
Using a constant width (as if rectangular) when the shape's width actually varies with depth
Not choosing an efficient substitution for the √(R^2-h^2) term

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the hydrostatic force on a plate that is inclined (not vertical), requiring a secant correction factor.
question_archetypes.example: A dam face is inclined at angle θ=30° to the vertical, length L=20 m, submerged to depth H=10 m. Find the total force.
question_archetypes.answer: dF=ρgh(L secθ)dh; F=ρg L secθ∫[0,H]h dh=ρgL secθ·H^2/2 = ρg(20)(sec30°)(50)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The plate/wall is explicitly described as inclined or slanted (not vertical) — the strip meets the surface along a slant, so its true width includes an extra secθ factor beyond the vertical depth range.
method_plan: Identify the incline angle θ from the vertical
Determine the slant-corrected strip width/length using secθ
Set up F=∫ρgh(slant width)dh and evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies the need for a secθ correction
M1: correct slant width expression
A1: correct integral setup
A1: correct evaluation

common_errors.description: Treating the inclined face as if it were vertical, omitting the secθ factor entirely
Using tanθ or sinθ instead of secθ for the slant correction
Not clearly stating which angle (from vertical vs. from horizontal) θ refers to

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the hydrostatic force on a plate that is submerged but does not reach the fluid surface (there is a gap between the surface and the top of the plate).
question_archetypes.example: A vertical square plate of side 2 m has its top edge 3 m below the water surface. Find the force.
question_archetypes.answer: Depth of a strip at local coordinate y (0≤y≤2 from the plate's top) is h=3+y; F=ρg·2∫[0,2](3+y)dy=ρg·2[3y+y^2/2]_0^2=ρg·2(6+2)=16ρg
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The plate is submerged below the surface with an explicit offset/gap given (top edge at some positive depth) rather than starting exactly at the surface — depth must include that offset.
method_plan: Set up a local coordinate along the plate and relate it to true depth h by adding the offset to the surface
Write the strip width as a function of the local coordinate
Set up F=∫ρgh·w dh (or using the local variable, adjusting the depth expression) and integrate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly relates local plate coordinate to true depth including the offset
M1: correct width function
A1: correct integral setup
A1: correct evaluation

common_errors.description: Forgetting the offset and integrating depth from 0 as if the plate's top were at the surface
Sign/arithmetic errors combining the offset with the local coordinate
Using the wrong limits for the local coordinate range

micro_skills.micro_skill: Work done by a variable force — Hooke's Law (springs)
definitions: For a variable force F(x) along the x-axis, work moving from x=a to x=b is W=∫[a,b]F(x)dx. Hooke's Law models a spring's restoring force as F(x)=kx, where x is displacement from natural length, giving W=∫[0,d]kx dx=½kd^2 to stretch/compress a distance d from natural length.

theorems.name: Work-energy integral / Hooke's Law
theorems.statement: W=∫[a,b]F(x)dx for a variable force F(x); for a spring, F(x)=kx (x = displacement from natural length), so W=½kd^2 to move from natural length to displacement d.
conditions: F(x) continuous
x measured as displacement from the spring's natural (unstretched) length

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a spring constant k and a stretch distance, find the work done to stretch (or compress) the spring.
question_archetypes.example: A spring has k=6 N/cm. Find the work to stretch it 10 cm from natural length.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The spring constant k is given directly (or trivially computable) and a single stretch distance from natural length is specified — direct application of W=½kd^2.
method_plan: Confirm the distance is measured from natural length
Apply W=∫[0,d]kx dx or W=½kd^2
Convert units if needed (e.g. N·cm to J)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct integral/formula setup
A1: correct evaluation
A1: correct unit conversion if required

common_errors.description: Measuring x from the wrong reference (e.g. from the stretched position instead of natural length)
Unit conversion errors (cm vs m, N·cm vs J)
Missing units in the final answer

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine the spring constant k from given force/displacement data, then compute work over a different interval.
question_archetypes.example: A spring has natural length 20 cm; a force of 30 N stretches it to 25 cm. Find the work to stretch it from 20 cm to 30 cm.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem gives one force/displacement data point rather than k directly, and/or asks for work over an interval that is not simply [0, given stretch] — requires first solving for k, then integrating over the correct interval.
method_plan: Use the given force/displacement pair to solve F=kx for k
Convert all displacements to a consistent unit and measure from natural length
Integrate kx over the requested displacement interval
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct k found from the given data point
M1: correct displacement interval identified (measured from natural length)
A1: correct integral setup
A1: correct evaluation with consistent units

common_errors.description: Using the given force as k directly instead of solving F=kx for k
Unit inconsistency between the given data and the requested interval
Integrating from the given data point's displacement instead of from 0 (natural length) when the problem asks for total work from natural length

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Handle a Hooke's Law problem involving compression (negative displacement) or a comparison between stretching and compressing.
question_archetypes.example: A spring with k=200 N/m has natural length 0.5 m. Find the work to compress it to 0.4 m, and compare to the work to stretch it to 0.6 m.
question_archetypes.answer: Compression: d=0.1 m, W=½(200)(0.1)^2=1 J; Stretch: d=0.1 m, W=1 J — same, since W depends only on |displacement|^2 from natural length
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem involves compression (displacement in the negative direction) or explicitly compares stretching vs. compressing the same spring — a chance to confuse signs or think the two require different work.
method_plan: Define displacement x as signed distance from natural length (negative for compression)
Set up W=∫kx dx over the correct signed interval, or use ½kd^2 with d=|displacement|
Compare stretch and compression cases, noting the formula depends only on d^2
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct signed displacement set up for compression
M1: correct work integral or ½kd^2 application
A1: correct numeric work for both cases
A1: correct conclusion that compression and equal-magnitude stretch require the same work

common_errors.description: Assuming compression requires different (or negative) work compared to stretching the same distance
Sign errors in setting up the integral limits for compression
Not explicitly stating the comparison/conclusion requested

micro_skills.micro_skill: Work to pump liquid out of a tank
definitions: To pump liquid out of a tank, slice the liquid into horizontal disks/washers at height h with volume element dV(h); the weight of that slice is dF=ρg dV(h), and lifting it a distance (H-h) to the rim at height H requires dW=ρg(H-h)dV(h); total work W=∫ρg(H-h)dV(h).

theorems.name: Work to pump liquid
theorems.statement: If a tank's horizontal cross-sectional area at height h is A(h), and liquid must be lifted to height H, W=∫ρg(H-h)A(h)dh over the liquid's depth range.
conditions: ρ (density) constant
A(h) is the horizontal cross-sectional area of the liquid at height h
each slice travels a distance depending on its own height, not a single constant distance

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the work to pump all the liquid out of a cylindrical (or other constant-cross-section) tank, full to the rim, up to the rim.
question_archetypes.example: A cylindrical tank of radius 2 m and height 5 m, full of water, is pumped out over the rim. Find the work.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The tank has a constant horizontal cross-section (cylinder, rectangular box) and is full to the rim, with liquid pumped exactly to the rim — the most direct pumping setup.
method_plan: Identify the constant cross-sectional area A
Set up W=ρg A∫(H-h)dh over the liquid's height range
Evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct constant area A
M1: correct (H-h) distance factor set up
A1: correct integral evaluation
A1: correct final numeric work with units

common_errors.description: Using a single constant lifting distance (e.g. the tank's full height) for every slice instead of (H-h) varying by height
Forgetting the ρg (weight density) factor, computing only a volume-like quantity
Missing units in the final answer

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the work to pump liquid that does not fill the tank completely, and/or must be lifted above the rim to an external point.
question_archetypes.example: A cylindrical tank of radius 2 m, height 5 m, is filled with water only to height 3 m, and must be pumped to a spout 1 m above the rim. Find the work.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem states the liquid level is below the top of the tank, and/or the discharge point is above the tank's rim — both change the correct value of H or the integration limits.
method_plan: Determine the correct upper limit of integration (the actual liquid surface, not necessarily the tank's top)
Determine the correct H (height liquid must be lifted to, possibly above the rim)
Set up and evaluate W=ρg A∫(H-h)dh with the corrected limits and H
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct integration limits matching the actual liquid depth
M1: correct H reflecting any lift above the rim
A1: correct integral setup
A1: correct evaluation

common_errors.description: Integrating over the full tank height even though the liquid doesn't fill it
Using the rim height as H even when the liquid must be lifted higher (to an elevated spout)
Errors evaluating ∫(H-h)dh over the corrected limits

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the work to pump liquid out of a tank whose cross-sectional area varies with height (e.g. cone or hemisphere tank).
question_archetypes.example: A conical tank (vertex down, apex at the bottom), radius R at the top, height H, is full of water and pumped out over the top. Find the work.
question_archetypes.answer: Radius at height h (measured from the apex) is r(h)=Rh/H, so A(h)=π(Rh/H)^2; W=ρg∫[0,H](H-h)π(Rh/H)^2dh = ρgπR^2/H^2 ∫[0,H](H-h)h^2dh = ρgπR^2H^2/12
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The tank's shape (cone, hemisphere, paraboloid) makes the cross-sectional area A(h) a genuinely varying function of height that must be derived using similar triangles or the shape's defining equation before setting up the pumping integral.
method_plan: Derive A(h) as a function of height using the tank's geometry (e.g. similar triangles for a cone)
Set up W=ρg∫(H-h)A(h)dh over the liquid's height range
Expand and integrate the resulting polynomial (or other) integrand
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct A(h) derived from the tank's shape
M1: correct (H-h) distance factor and integral setup
A1: correct expansion/integration
A1: correct final evaluation

common_errors.description: Errors deriving r(h) via similar triangles (e.g. inverting the ratio)
Using a constant cross-sectional area (as if cylindrical) for a tank whose shape actually varies with height
Not expanding (H-h)h^2 before integrating, leading to avoidable algebra errors

micro_skills.micro_skill: Work against a variable (inverse-square) gravitational force
definitions: The gravitational force on a mass m at height h above a planet's surface (radius R) is F(h)=Km/(R+h)^2. The work to raise m from the surface to height H is W=∫[0,H]F(h)dh=Km(1/R-1/(R+H)); as H→∞, W→Km/R (finite, despite an infinite distance).

theorems.name: Work against inverse-square gravity
theorems.statement: W=∫[0,H]Km/(R+h)^2 dh=Km(1/R-1/(R+H)). Taking H→∞ gives the finite value W=Km/R.
conditions: F(h)=Km/(R+h)^2 with K a constant (K=gR^2 if F=mg at h=0)
h measured as height above the surface, R the planet's radius

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the work needed to raise a mass against gravity from a planet's surface to a given finite height.
question_archetypes.example: Find the work to raise a 10 kg mass from Earth's surface (R≈6.4×10^6 m) to height H=6.4×10^6 m (i.e., to 2R), given g=9.8 m/s^2.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A finite height H above the surface is given (not 'to infinity'), and the constant K must first be related to g and R via F(0)=mg.
method_plan: Determine K from F(0)=mg, giving K=gR^2
Set up W=∫[0,H]Km/(R+h)^2dh and evaluate, or use the closed form W=Km(1/R-1/(R+H))
Substitute numeric values
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly relates K to g and R (K=gR^2)
M1: correct integral or closed-form setup
A1: correct algebraic simplification
A1: correct numeric evaluation

common_errors.description: Using the constant surface value F=mg for all heights instead of the true 1/(R+h)^2 variation
Errors simplifying 1/R-1/(R+H) algebraically
Forgetting K depends on g and R and must be computed, not assumed to be a given constant

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the work to raise a mass to an effectively infinite height (escape from the gravitational field), and connect it to escape velocity via energy conservation.
question_archetypes.example: Show that escape velocity from a planet of radius R, surface gravity g, is v=√(2gR), and compute it for Earth.
question_archetypes.answer: W(∞)=Km/R=gRm (using K=gR^2); setting ½mv^2=gRm (all kinetic energy converts to overcome gravity to infinity) gives v=√(2gR)≈√(2·9.8·6.4×10^6)≈1.12×10^4 m/s
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks for work 'to infinity' or for escape velocity — this is the H→∞ limit of the finite-height work formula, connected to kinetic energy via conservation of energy.
method_plan: Take the limit H→∞ in W=Km(1/R-1/(R+H)) to get W(∞)=Km/R
Set the required kinetic energy ½mv^2 equal to this work (energy conservation)
Solve for v and evaluate numerically
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct limit W(∞)=Km/R=gRm
M1: correct energy-conservation equation ½mv^2=gRm
A1: correct algebraic solution for v
A1: correct numeric evaluation, noting v is independent of mass

common_errors.description: Not taking the limit correctly, e.g. treating 1/(R+H) as zero prematurely without justification
Forgetting escape velocity is independent of the object's own mass (mass cancels)
Errors solving ½mv^2=gRm for v (forgetting the factor of 2 under the square root)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the additional work required to move a mass between two nonzero heights above the surface (not starting from the surface).
question_archetypes.example: Find the work to raise a mass m from height H1=R to height H2=3R above a planet's surface (R = planet radius), using F(h)=Km/(R+h)^2.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Both the starting and ending heights are nonzero (neither is the surface, h=0), so the work integral's limits must both be adjusted rather than assuming the object starts at the surface.
method_plan: Set up the work integral with the correct nonzero starting and ending heights as limits
Integrate F(h)=Km/(R+h)^2
Evaluate at both limits and subtract
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct limits of integration reflecting both nonzero heights
M1: correct antiderivative -Km/(R+h)
A1: correct evaluation at both limits
A1: correct final simplified work

common_errors.description: Assuming the object starts at the surface (h=0) when the problem specifies a nonzero starting height
Sign errors evaluating the antiderivative at the upper vs. lower limit
Not simplifying the final fraction

micro_skills.micro_skill: Potential/kinetic energy and conservation of energy from work integrals
definitions: Work done against a position-dependent force F(x) moving from a to b is stored as potential energy P.E.=-∫[a,b]F(x)dx; kinetic energy is K.E.=½mv^2. Using Newton's Second Law (F=m dv/dt=mv dv/dx), one derives P.E.(b)+K.E.(b)=P.E.(a)+K.E.(a) — conservation of energy — whenever F depends only on position (a conservative force).

theorems.name: Conservation of energy
theorems.statement: If F(x) depends only on position (conservative), then P.E.(x)+K.E.(x) is constant along the motion, where P.E.(x)=-∫F(x)dx (up to an additive constant) and K.E.=½mv^2.
conditions: F depends only on position x, not on time or velocity explicitly (conservative force)
motion governed by Newton's Second Law F=ma

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Derive the conservation-of-energy statement from Newton's Second Law and the work integral.
question_archetypes.example: Starting from F=mv dv/dx, show that P.E.(b)+K.E.(b)=P.E.(a)+K.E.(a) for a conservative force F(x).
question_archetypes.answer: ∫[a,b]F dx=∫[a,b]mv(dv/dx)dx=∫m v dv=½m[v(b)^2-v(a)^2]=K.E.(b)-K.E.(a); also ∫[a,b]F dx=-[P.E.(b)-P.E.(a)] by definition, so K.E.(b)-K.E.(a)=-(P.E.(b)-P.E.(a)), i.e. P.E.(b)+K.E.(b)=P.E.(a)+K.E.(a)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem explicitly asks to derive or prove the conservation law, not just apply it — requires connecting F=ma to F=mv dv/dx and matching both sides to the P.E./K.E. definitions.
method_plan: Rewrite Newton's Second Law as F=mv dv/dx (chain rule on v(x(t)))
Integrate both sides of F=mv dv/dx from a to b, recognizing the K.E. change on the right
Equate to the work integral, which by definition is -(change in P.E.), and rearrange
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct chain-rule rewriting F=m dv/dt=mv dv/dx
M1: correct integration giving the K.E. difference
A1: correctly links the same integral to -(ΔP.E.) by definition
A1: correct final rearrangement to the conservation statement

common_errors.description: Not recognizing dv/dt=v dv/dx as the key chain-rule step connecting force and the K.E. integral
Sign errors when moving P.E. and K.E. terms between sides of the equation
Not clearly stating the assumption that F depends only on position (conservative)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Apply conservation of energy to find a speed or height given known force/work data, without re-deriving the theorem.
question_archetypes.example: A 2 kg object is dropped from height 10 m (ignore air resistance, g=9.8). Use conservation of energy to find its speed on impact.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem gives enough information to compute a change in potential energy (height, mass, force) and asks for a resulting speed (or vice versa) — a direct application of P.E.+K.E.=constant.
method_plan: Compute the change in potential energy between the two states
Set it equal to the change in kinetic energy (with opposite sign convention as needed)
Solve for the unknown speed or height
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct P.E. change computed
M1: correct K.E. expression set up
A1: correct algebraic solution for the unknown
A1: correct final numeric answer

common_errors.description: Sign confusion between P.E. lost and K.E. gained (or vice versa)
Errors solving for v from v^2 (forgetting the square root, or including a spurious negative root)
Forgetting to account for an initial nonzero speed or height if given

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Correctly apply the sign convention P.E.=-∫F dx in a scenario where getting the sign wrong would flip the direction of energy transfer.
question_archetypes.example: A ball is thrown upward against gravity F=-mg (taking up as positive x). Show P.E.=mgx (not -mgx) using P.E.=-∫F dx.
question_archetypes.answer: P.E.=-∫(-mg)dx=∫mg dx=mgx+C; taking P.E.=0 at x=0 gives P.E.=mgx, correctly increasing with height
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The force is given with an explicit sign (e.g. gravity acting in the negative direction) and the problem tests whether the student correctly threads that sign through the P.E.=-∫F dx definition rather than dropping or double-applying a minus sign.
method_plan: Write F(x) with its correct sign convention relative to the chosen positive direction
Apply P.E.=-∫F(x)dx carefully, keeping track of the sign
Check the result makes physical sense (e.g. P.E. should increase with height under gravity)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct signed force expression
M1: correct application of the P.E.=-∫F dx definition
A1: correct resulting P.E. expression
A1: sanity check confirming P.E. increases/decreases in the physically expected direction

common_errors.description: Dropping or double-applying the negative sign in P.E.=-∫F dx
Not understanding why the minus sign exists (work done against F stores positive energy)
Not checking the final P.E. expression against physical intuition (e.g. increasing with height under gravity)

micro_skills.micro_skill: Recovering total quantities from marginal rate functions
definitions: If f'(x) is a known 'marginal' rate (marginal revenue, marginal cost, marginal profit) per unit x, then the total change f(b)-f(a)=∫[a,b]f'(x)dx recovers the total revenue/cost/profit over that range, by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

theorems.name: Marginal-to-total via FTC
theorems.statement: If R'(x) is marginal revenue, total revenue from selling units a through b is R(b)-R(a)=∫[a,b]R'(x)dx (similarly for cost, profit).
conditions: R' (or the relevant marginal function) continuous on [a,b]

formulas: profit=revenue-cost, so marginal profit = marginal revenue - marginal cost

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a marginal revenue (or cost) function, find total revenue (or cost) over a range of units.
question_archetypes.example: Marginal revenue is 15-5e^{-x/50} dollars per unit after x units sold. Find total revenue from the first 100 units.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem gives a function explicitly labelled 'marginal' (revenue, cost, or profit) and asks for a total or cumulative quantity over a range — integrate the marginal function.
method_plan: Recognize the marginal function should be integrated, not evaluated pointwise
Set up the definite integral over the given unit range
Evaluate, including any necessary exponential/other antiderivative
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly sets up the definite integral of the marginal function
M1: correct antiderivative
A1: correct evaluation at both limits
A1: correct final numeric total with appropriate units/rounding

common_errors.description: Evaluating the marginal function at a single point (e.g. x=100) instead of integrating it over the range
Errors with the exponential antiderivative or evaluation
Not rounding/presenting the final dollar amount clearly

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Combine marginal revenue and marginal cost to find total profit over a range, or find the profit-maximizing quantity.
question_archetypes.example: Marginal revenue is R'(x)=50-0.1x and marginal cost is C'(x)=20+0.05x. Find the total profit from producing and selling the first 200 units.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Both a marginal revenue and a marginal cost function are given, requiring the student to first form marginal profit (their difference) before integrating for total profit.
method_plan: Form marginal profit P'(x)=R'(x)-C'(x)
Integrate P'(x) over the given range
Evaluate to get total profit
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly forms P'(x)=R'(x)-C'(x)
M1: correct integral setup
A1: correct antiderivative
A1: correct evaluation

common_errors.description: Integrating R' and C' separately and subtracting the wrong quantities, or forgetting profit is R-C not R+C
Errors combining R'(x) and C'(x) into P'(x)
Not recognizing this reduces to the same 'integrate the marginal function' idea already used for revenue alone

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize and evaluate an improper integral arising from a marginal function integrated over an unbounded range (e.g. lifetime revenue/cost).
question_archetypes.example: Marginal revenue from an ongoing subscription service is R'(x)=100e^{-0.01x} dollars per additional 1000 subscribers, for all x≥0. Find the total revenue achievable in the long run (x→∞).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The range of integration is unbounded (a 'total over all time/units' or 'long-run' phrasing) — the marginal-to-total integral becomes improper and must be checked for convergence.
method_plan: Set up the marginal-to-total integral with an infinite upper limit
Rewrite as a limit of a proper integral
Evaluate the limit and state whether the total is finite or infinite
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly rewrote as a limit of a proper integral
M1: correct antiderivative
A1: correct limit evaluation
A1: correct conclusion (finite value or divergence) stated clearly

common_errors.description: Plugging in ∞ directly rather than taking a limit
Assuming a marginal function that never reaches zero must give infinite total revenue
Not recognizing the connection to improper integral convergence tests from earlier in the course

micro_skills.micro_skill: Present value of a continuous income stream
definitions: With continuously compounded discount rate δ, a payment of $1 received t years from now is worth e^{-δt} today. If income arrives at rate P(t) dollars/year over [0,T], the present value is V=∫[0,T]e^{-δt}P(t)dt.

theorems.name: Present value of a continuous stream
theorems.statement: V=∫[0,T]e^{-δt}P(t)dt for income at rate P(t) over [0,T]; for a perpetual stream, V=∫[0,∞)e^{-δt}P(t)dt (an improper integral).
conditions: δ>0 is the continuously compounded discount rate
P(t) continuous, represents dollars per year

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the present value of a continuous income stream with constant rate over a finite time horizon.
question_archetypes.example: Find the present value of a $5000/year income stream for 20 years at discount rate 8%.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A constant income rate and a finite number of years are given along with a discount rate — direct substitution into the finite-horizon present value formula.
method_plan: Set up V=∫[0,T]e^{-δt}P dt with the given P, δ, T
Integrate (exponential antiderivative)
Evaluate at both limits
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct integral setup with correct δ (percentage converted to decimal)
M1: correct antiderivative
A1: correct evaluation at both limits
A1: correct final numeric present value

common_errors.description: Forgetting to convert a percentage discount rate to decimal form
Integrating e^{-δt} incorrectly (sign error in the antiderivative)
Not rounding/presenting the dollar amount sensibly

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the present value of a perpetual (never-ending) constant income stream, requiring an improper integral.
question_archetypes.example: Find the present value of a perpetual $10,000/year income stream at discount rate 6%.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The income stream is described as perpetual, forever, or indefinite (no finite end date given) — the present-value integral has an infinite upper limit.
method_plan: Set up the present-value integral with an infinite upper limit
Rewrite as a limit of a proper integral over [0,R]
Evaluate the limit, noting the exponential decay guarantees convergence
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies the need for an improper integral
M1: correct limit setup
A1: correct evaluation showing convergence
A1: correct final present value

common_errors.description: Treating the perpetual stream as if it had some implicit finite T instead of taking T→∞
Not recognizing why the integral converges here (e^{-δt} decays faster than the constant P grows, since P is constant)
Sign error evaluating the antiderivative's limit as t→∞

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the present value of an income stream whose rate P(t) varies with time (not constant), requiring integration by parts or another technique.
question_archetypes.example: Find the present value of an income stream growing linearly, P(t)=1000+200t dollars/year, over 10 years at discount rate 5%.
question_archetypes.answer: V=∫[0,10]e^{-0.05t}(1000+200t)dt = 1000∫e^{-0.05t}dt+200∫te^{-0.05t}dt, the second requiring integration by parts
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The income rate P(t) is given as a non-constant function of time (linear, exponential growth, seasonal, etc.), so the present-value integral is not the simple constant-rate closed form and needs its own integration technique.
method_plan: Split the integral according to the terms in P(t) if it's a sum
Apply the appropriate technique (e.g. integration by parts for a t·e^{-δt} term)
Evaluate each piece and sum, then simplify
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly sets up ∫e^{-δt}P(t)dt with the full (non-constant) P(t)
M1: correctly applies integration by parts (or another needed technique) to the non-constant part
A1: correct antiderivative
A1: correct evaluation and final present value

common_errors.description: Using the constant-rate closed form V=(P/δ)(1-e^{-δT}) when P(t) is not actually constant
Errors in the integration-by-parts setup for the te^{-δt} term (wrong choice of u and dv)
Sign or arithmetic errors combining the two integral pieces

micro_skills.micro_skill: Renewable-resource economics: logistic growth and harvesting
definitions: A population with logistic growth dx/dt=kx(1-x/L), harvested at rate h(t), satisfies dx/dt=kx(1-x/L)-h(t). Harvesting exactly at the growth rate keeps the population constant; income T=pkx(1-x/L) (price p per unit) is maximized over x at x=L/2. With a continuous discount rate δ on future income, the income-maximizing equilibrium population becomes x*=(k-δ)L/(2k), smaller than L/2, and if δ≥k the model recommends harvesting to extinction immediately.

theorems.name: Optimal sustainable harvest population
theorems.statement: For logistic growth rate kx(1-x/L), the sustainable harvest income pkx(1-x/L) is maximized at x=L/2 (undiscounted); with discount rate δ, the optimum shifts to x*=(k-δ)L/(2k).
conditions: harvest rate exactly matches growth rate (population held at equilibrium x)
k>0 (intrinsic growth rate), L>0 (carrying capacity)

formulas: sustainable income T(x)=pkx(1-x/L), maximized at x=L/2

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the harvest rate that keeps a logistically growing population at a fixed equilibrium level.
question_archetypes.example: A fish population grows logistically with k=0.4/year, L=10,000. Find the sustainable harvest rate to keep the population fixed at x=6000.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem specifies both a fixed target population level and asks for the matching harvest rate — direct substitution into h=kx(1-x/L) since dx/dt=0 at equilibrium requires harvest to exactly equal growth.
method_plan: Recall that a constant population requires harvest rate = growth rate at that population level
Substitute the given x into kx(1-x/L)
Evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly sets harvest rate equal to the logistic growth rate at the given x
A1: correct substitution and evaluation

common_errors.description: Not recognizing that a constant population requires dx/dt=0, i.e. harvest exactly cancels growth
Errors evaluating kx(1-x/L)
Not stating units (fish/year, kg/year, etc.)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the population level that maximizes sustainable harvesting income (undiscounted), using calculus (maximize T(x)=pkx(1-x/L)).
question_archetypes.example: Show the income T(x)=pkx(1-x/L) is maximized at x=L/2, and find the maximum income for p=$5, k=0.4, L=10,000.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks to find the income-maximizing population level itself (an optimization problem), distinct from just applying the harvest-rate formula at a given x.
method_plan: Write the income function T(x)=pkx(1-x/L)
Differentiate and set T'(x)=0 to find the critical point
Verify it's a maximum and evaluate T there
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct income function set up
M1: correct derivative and critical point x=L/2
A1: verification that this is a maximum (e.g. second derivative or sign check)
A1: correct maximum income value

common_errors.description: Forgetting to verify the critical point is a maximum (not just setting derivative to zero)
Errors differentiating T(x)=pkx(1-x/L)
Confusing 'population that maximizes income' with 'population with maximum growth rate' (these coincide here but the reasoning should be income-based)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Incorporate a continuous discount rate into the harvesting-optimization model and interpret the resulting shift in optimal population (including the extinction-risk case).
question_archetypes.example: For k=0.3/year, L=10,000, and discount rate δ=0.1, find the discounted income-maximizing population x*, and explain what happens if δ≥k.
question_archetypes.answer: x*=(k-δ)L/(2k)=(0.3-0.1)(10,000)/(0.6)≈3333, smaller than L/2=5000; if δ≥k, x*≤0, meaning the model recommends harvesting to extinction immediately since any surviving population is 'worth more' harvested now than preserved
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A discount rate δ is explicitly introduced alongside the logistic harvesting model, and/or the problem asks to interpret what happens for large δ relative to k — a conceptual economics-meets-calculus synthesis question.
method_plan: Substitute k, L, δ into x*=(k-δ)L/(2k)
Compare x* to the undiscounted optimum L/2
Discuss the extinction case δ≥k and its real-world implication
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution into x*=(k-δ)L/(2k)
A1: correct numeric comparison to L/2
A1: correct qualitative discussion of the δ≥k extinction scenario
presentation: connects the math result to the sustainability implication

common_errors.description: Not recognizing why a higher discount rate pushes the optimal population down (future growth is worth less than present harvest)
Errors substituting into the x* formula
Treating this as a pure algebra plug-in without addressing the requested interpretation/discussion

micro_skills.micro_skill: Discrete random variables: mean and variance
definitions: A discrete random variable X has probability function f(x)=Pr(X=x) with Σf(x)=1. The mean is μ=E(X)=Σx f(x), and more generally E(g(X))=Σg(x)f(x). The variance is σ^2=Var(X)=E[(X-μ)^2]=Σ(x-μ)^2f(x)=E(X^2)-μ^2, and σ=√Var(X).

theorems.name: Mean and variance (discrete)
theorems.statement: μ=E(X)=Σx f(x); σ^2=E(X^2)-μ^2, with E(X^2)=Σx^2 f(x).
conditions: f(x)≥0 for all x in the range
Σf(x)=1 over the range

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the mean and variance of a discrete random variable given its full probability function.
question_archetypes.example: X = sum of two fair dice, 2≤X≤12. Find μ=E(X) and σ^2.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A complete probability function/table (or a well-known discrete distribution like a dice sum) is given, and mean and/or variance are requested directly.
method_plan: List or determine f(x) for each value of x
Compute μ=Σx f(x)
Compute E(X^2)=Σx^2f(x) and use σ^2=E(X^2)-μ^2
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct probability function values
M1: correct μ computed
A1: correct E(X^2)
A1: correct σ^2 (and σ if requested)

common_errors.description: Using σ^2=Σ(x-μ)^2f(x) directly with arithmetic slips instead of the more efficient E(X^2)-μ^2 shortcut
Arithmetic errors summing the weighted values
Forgetting to weight each x by its probability rather than just averaging the raw x-values

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find a missing/unknown probability value in a probability function using the normalization condition Σf(x)=1.
question_archetypes.example: A random variable X has f(1)=0.2, f(2)=0.3, f(3)=c, f(4)=0.1. Find c.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A probability table or function is given with one value replaced by an unknown constant, and the normalization condition Σf(x)=1 is the key tool to solve for it.
method_plan: Write the equation Σf(x)=1 including the unknown
Solve for the unknown constant
Optionally verify all f(x)≥0
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct normalization equation set up
A1: correct solved value
A1: verification that resulting probabilities are all valid (≥0, ≤1)

common_errors.description: Forgetting the normalization condition and guessing/leaving the value undetermined
Arithmetic slip solving the linear equation
Not checking the found value gives a valid probability (between 0 and 1)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Compute the expectation of a function of a discrete random variable, E(g(X)), not just E(X) itself.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks for the expectation of an explicit function of X (e.g. X^2, 2X+1, X^2-1), not simply E(X) — apply E(g(X))=Σg(x)f(x) directly with g, not X itself.
method_plan: Identify g(x) as given in the problem
Compute g(x) at each value of x in the support
Weight each g(x) by f(x) and sum
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct g(x) values computed at each support point
M1: correct weighting by f(x)
A1: correct sum/final expectation

common_errors.description: Computing g(E(X)) instead of E(g(X)) (these are generally different for nonlinear g)
Errors evaluating g(x) at each point
Forgetting to include all values in the support of X

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use the variance shortcut formula σ^2=E(X^2)-μ^2 in a case where computing Σ(x-μ)^2f(x) directly would be considerably more work, and verify the two methods agree.
question_archetypes.example: For a random variable with a non-symmetric distribution over 5+ values, compute σ^2 both via the definition Σ(x-μ)^2f(x) and via E(X^2)-μ^2, confirming they match.
question_archetypes.answer: Both methods should yield the same σ^2 (e.g. σ^2=4.2); the shortcut typically requires less arithmetic since it avoids expanding (x-μ)^2 for each of many values
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A distribution has several possible values (making direct expansion of (x-μ)^2 for each tedious), and the problem may explicitly ask to verify or compare both variance computation methods.
method_plan: Compute μ once
Compute σ^2 via the definition Σ(x-μ)^2f(x) directly
Compute σ^2 via the shortcut E(X^2)-μ^2 and confirm the two match
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct μ
M1: correct direct computation via the definition
A1: correct shortcut computation via E(X^2)-μ^2
A1: explicit confirmation the two methods agree

common_errors.description: Always using the more laborious direct definition even when many values make the shortcut clearly more efficient
Errors in either the direct expansion or the E(X^2) computation
Not explicitly comparing/confirming the two methods give the same result when asked to verify

micro_skills.micro_skill: Continuous densities: normalization and probability as area
definitions: A probability density function (pdf) f on [a,b] satisfies f≥0 and ∫[a,b]f(x)dx=1; then Pr(x1≤X≤x2)=∫[x1,x2]f(x)dx. A candidate function must first be checked/normalized (solved for an unknown constant so the total integral equals 1) before it can be used as a density.

theorems.name: Density normalization
theorems.statement: f is a valid pdf on [a,b] iff f(x)≥0 for all x in [a,b] and ∫[a,b]f(x)dx=1.
conditions: domain [a,b] may be infinite (improper integral then required)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the normalizing constant C so a given candidate function becomes a valid probability density on a specified interval.
question_archetypes.example: For what C is f(x)=C(1-x^2) a density on [-1,1]?
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A function with an unknown constant is given along with an interval, and the problem asks for the value of the constant that makes it a valid density — set the total integral equal to 1 and solve.
method_plan: Set up ∫[a,b]f(x)dx=1 with the unknown constant included
Evaluate the integral in terms of the constant
Solve for the constant
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct integral set up equal to 1
M1: correct evaluation of the integral
A1: correct solved constant

common_errors.description: Errors evaluating the integral (e.g. of 1-x^2 over a symmetric interval)
Forgetting to check f(x)≥0 over the interval with the found constant
Setting the integral equal to something other than 1

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Using a normalized density, compute the probability that X falls in a specified sub-interval.
question_archetypes.example: With f(x)=¾(1-x^2) on [-1,1] (already normalized), find Pr(X≤½).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The density is given (already normalized or normalization is a preliminary step) and the question asks for the probability over a specific sub-interval — integrate f over that sub-interval, not the whole domain.
method_plan: Confirm or first find the normalizing constant
Set up ∫ over the requested sub-interval
Evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: uses the correctly normalized density
M1: correct sub-interval limits
A1: correct integral evaluation
A1: probability value between 0 and 1 (sanity check)

common_errors.description: Forgetting to first normalize the density before computing the probability
Errors with the limits of integration for the requested sub-interval
Not sanity-checking the final probability lies in [0,1]

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine whether a given function (with no free constant, or with a stated constant) is or is not a valid probability density, identifying which condition fails if it isn't.
question_archetypes.example: Is f(x)=2x on [0,1] a valid density? Is g(x)=x on [-1,1] a valid density?
question_archetypes.answer: f(x)=2x on [0,1]: f≥0 on [0,1] and ∫[0,1]2x dx=1 — valid. g(x)=x on [-1,1]: g<0 for x<0, so g fails the nonnegativity condition — NOT valid, regardless of its integral.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The function is presented without an adjustable constant (so 'find C' doesn't apply) and the task is to verify both conditions (nonnegativity and total integral =1) rather than assume validity.
method_plan: Check f(x)≥0 over the entire stated domain
Check ∫f(x)dx=1 over the domain
Conclude valid/invalid, citing which condition (if any) fails
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly checks the nonnegativity condition over the full domain
M1: correctly checks/evaluates the total integral
A1: correct valid/invalid conclusion
A1: correctly identifies which specific condition fails when invalid

common_errors.description: Checking only the integral-equals-1 condition and ignoring the nonnegativity requirement (or vice versa)
Checking nonnegativity only at an endpoint or a few sample points rather than the whole domain
Concluding 'invalid' without stating which specific condition failed

micro_skills.micro_skill: Mean and variance of continuous random variables (including uniform and exponential)
definitions: For a continuous rv with density f on [a,b], μ=E(X)=∫[a,b]xf(x)dx and σ^2=E(X^2)-μ^2=∫[a,b]x^2f(x)dx-μ^2. Uniform on [a,b]: f(x)=1/(b-a), μ=(a+b)/2, σ=(b-a)/(2√3). Exponential on [0,∞): f(x)=ke^{-kx} (k>0), μ=σ=1/k.

theorems.name: Continuous mean/variance
theorems.statement: μ=∫xf(x)dx, σ^2=∫x^2f(x)dx-μ^2, for a continuous rv with density f. Special cases: Uniform[a,b] has μ=(a+b)/2, σ=(b-a)/(2√3); Exponential(k) has μ=σ=1/k.
conditions: density f properly normalized (∫f=1) on its domain
for exponential, domain [0,∞) and k>0

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the mean and variance of a continuous random variable given a general (non-named) density function.
question_archetypes.example: X has density f(x)=3x^2 on [0,1] (already normalized). Find μ and σ^2.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A specific (often polynomial) density function is given directly, and mean and variance are requested — set up and evaluate the two defining integrals.
method_plan: Set up μ=∫xf(x)dx and evaluate
Set up E(X^2)=∫x^2f(x)dx and evaluate
Compute σ^2=E(X^2)-μ^2
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct μ integral and evaluation
M1: correct E(X^2) integral and evaluation
A1: correct σ^2 via the shortcut formula
A1: correct final numeric values, sensible given the domain

common_errors.description: Forgetting to first check/establish the density is normalized before computing moments
Errors integrating xf(x) or x^2f(x)
Using σ^2=E(X^2) instead of E(X^2)-μ^2

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Apply the known uniform-distribution mean/variance formulas directly.
question_archetypes.example: X is uniformly distributed on [2,10]. Find μ and σ.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The random variable is explicitly stated to be uniformly distributed on a given interval — apply the standard formulas rather than integrating from scratch.
method_plan: Identify a and b from the given interval
Apply μ=(a+b)/2 and σ=(b-a)/(2√3)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of a, b
A1: correct μ and σ from the formulas

common_errors.description: Mixing up a and b or misapplying the formula
Re-deriving from scratch via integration instead of using the known uniform formulas (not wrong, but inefficient and error-prone under time pressure)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Apply the exponential distribution's mean/variance formulas, and connect k to a real-world rate parameter.
question_archetypes.example: The time between radioactive decays follows an exponential distribution with mean 5 minutes. Find k and Pr(T≤2).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A real-world waiting-time or lifetime scenario is described (radioactive decay, equipment failure) with a given mean, cueing the exponential distribution and its μ=1/k relationship.
method_plan: Recognize the exponential distribution applies and identify k from the given mean via μ=1/k
Set up the probability as ∫[0,t]ke^{-ks}ds or use Pr(T≤t)=1-e^{-kt} directly
Evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies k from the given mean
M1: correct probability integral or formula used
A1: correct evaluation
A1: sensible final probability value

common_errors.description: Confusing k with the mean itself instead of k=1/mean
Re-deriving Pr(T≤t)=1-e^{-kt} from scratch each time instead of recalling it, risking sign errors
Errors evaluating 1-e^{-kt} numerically

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize a distribution for which the mean and/or variance do not exist (a heavy-tailed distribution), and explain why the defining integral diverges.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why the Cauchy distribution C(x)=(1/π)·γ/((x-μ0)^2+γ^2) has no finite mean or variance.
question_archetypes.answer: E(X) requires ∫x·C(x)dx over (-∞,∞); the integrand behaves like 1/x for large |x|, and ∫1/x dx diverges (logarithmically) — the integral does not converge absolutely, so E(X) (and hence the variance) does not exist
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The named distribution is one known for heavy tails (Cauchy, or another explicitly described as having tails that decay slowly, e.g. like a power law), and the question asks about existence of moments rather than their numeric value.
method_plan: Write the defining integral for the mean (or variance)
Examine the tail behaviour of the integrand as x→±∞
Determine whether the integral converges absolutely; conclude the moment exists or fails to exist
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly sets up the mean (or variance) integral for the given density
M1: correctly analyzes the tail decay rate of the integrand
A1: correct convergence/divergence conclusion
A1: clear explanation connecting decay rate to existence of the moment

common_errors.description: Assuming every valid probability density automatically has a finite mean and variance
Attempting to force a numeric answer via symmetry (e.g. claiming mean=μ0 by symmetry) without addressing that the integral doesn't converge absolutely
Not clearly explaining the comparison test / tail-decay reasoning behind the divergence

micro_skills.micro_skill: The normal distribution: standardizing and probability calculations
definitions: The standard normal density is f(z)=(1/√(2π))e^{-z^2/2}, mean 0, sd 1. A general normal X with mean μ, sd σ has density f_{μ,σ}(x)=(1/σ)f((x-μ)/σ). Standardize via Z=(X-μ)/σ, then use the cumulative distribution function F(z)=Pr(Z≤z)=(1/√(2π))∫_{-∞}^z e^{-t^2/2}dt, found from a standard normal table or via the error function F(z)=½(erf(z/√2)+1).

theorems.name: Standardization
theorems.statement: If X~Normal(μ,σ), then Z=(X-μ)/σ ~ Normal(0,1), and Pr(X≤x)=Pr(Z≤(x-μ)/σ)=F((x-μ)/σ).
conditions: F is the standard normal cdf, typically read from a table

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Standardize and find the probability that a normal random variable falls within a given range.
question_archetypes.example: X~Normal(μ=2,σ=0.4). Find Pr(1.8≤X≤2.4).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A normal random variable with given mean and standard deviation is specified, and the probability of falling in an interval is requested — standardize both endpoints and use the table.
method_plan: Convert both endpoints to Z-scores using Z=(x-μ)/σ
Look up F at each Z-score
Subtract to get the interval probability
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct Z-scores for both endpoints
M1: correct table values used
A1: correct subtraction
A1: sensible final probability (between 0 and 1)

common_errors.description: Errors computing the Z-scores
Subtracting F-values in the wrong order (upper minus lower)
Forgetting F(-z)=1-F(z) when a table only lists nonnegative z

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find a one-sided (upper or lower tail) probability for a normal random variable, using Pr(X>x)=1-F(z).
question_archetypes.example: X~Normal(100,15) (an IQ-type score). Find Pr(X>130), given F(2)≈0.977.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks for the probability of exceeding (or falling below) a single threshold, not a two-sided range — requires the complement rule Pr(X>x)=1-F(z) rather than a direct table lookup interpreted as an upper-tail probability.
method_plan: Standardize the threshold to get z
Look up F(z) from the table (a lower-tail/cumulative value)
Use 1-F(z) for an upper-tail probability (or F(z) directly for a lower-tail one)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct Z-score
M1: correctly identifies whether the tail needed is upper or lower
A1: correct application of the complement rule if needed
A1: correct final probability

common_errors.description: Using F(z) directly as if it were the upper-tail probability, forgetting F is the cumulative (lower-tail) probability
Errors in the Z-score computation
Not stating the probability as a percentage or clarifying its practical meaning when asked to interpret

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a probability, find the corresponding value of X (an inverse normal problem), using the table in reverse.
question_archetypes.example: X~Normal(500,100) (e.g. a test score). Find the score x such that Pr(X≤x)=0.90, given F(1.28)≈0.90.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem gives a probability (percentile) and asks for the corresponding X-value, rather than giving an X-value and asking for a probability — an inverse lookup, converting z back to x via x=μ+zσ.
method_plan: Look up (or use the given) z-value corresponding to the target cumulative probability
Convert back to X using x=μ+zσ
State the final value in the original units/context
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies the target cumulative probability and finds the matching z (via table or given value)
M1: correct formula x=μ+zσ used to invert
A1: correct final numeric x-value
A1: contextually sensible interpretation of the result

common_errors.description: Confusing the direction of the lookup — using x=σz+μ with a z found from the wrong cumulative direction (e.g. using the 10th percentile's z when the 90th was wanted)
Errors substituting into x=μ+zσ
Not recognizing this requires the inverse of the same standardization formula used in forward problems

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Set up (and interpret, without necessarily evaluating numerically) a probability as an integral of the normal density, connecting the table-based shortcut to its integral definition.
question_archetypes.example: Write Pr(1≤X≤3) for X~Normal(2,1) as a definite integral of the normal density, and explain how F converts it to a table lookup.
question_archetypes.answer: Pr(1≤X≤3)=∫[1,3](1/√(2π))e^{-(x-2)^2/2}dx = F((3-2)/1)-F((1-2)/1)=F(1)-F(-1), since substituting z=(x-2)/1 turns the integral into a standard-normal cdf difference
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem explicitly asks to connect the probability to its integral definition (e.g. 'write as an integral', 'derive', or 'explain why the table method works') rather than just compute a numeric answer via the table.
method_plan: Write the probability as a definite integral of the general normal density f_{μ,σ}(x)
Substitute z=(x-μ)/σ to transform it into an integral of the standard normal density
Identify the transformed integral as F(z_2)-F(z_1)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct general normal density integral written down
M1: correct substitution z=(x-μ)/σ shown explicitly
A1: correctly identifies the result as a difference of standard normal cdf values
presentation: clearly explains why standardizing lets any normal probability reduce to a single table

common_errors.description: Treating the table lookup as a memorized shortcut without understanding it comes from the z-substitution in the integral
Errors in the substitution (e.g. wrong differential dz=dx/σ)
Jumping straight to F(z2)-F(z1) without showing the underlying integral/substitution when the problem explicitly asks for it

micro_skills.micro_skill: Separable equations: general solution
definitions: A first-order equation dy/dx=f(x)g(y) is separable: rewrite as dy/g(y)=f(x)dx and integrate both sides. Constant solutions y=C where g(C)=0 solve the equation trivially but can be lost by dividing by g(y) during separation, so they must be checked separately after solving.

theorems.name: Separation of variables
theorems.statement: If dy/dx=f(x)g(y) with g(y)≠0, then ∫dy/g(y)=∫f(x)dx defines the general solution implicitly (or explicitly after solving for y); any constant solution y=C with g(C)=0 must be checked and added if not already contained in the general solution's constant.
conditions: f, g continuous
division by g(y) requires g(y)≠0, so constant solutions g(C)=0 need separate verification

formulas: constant solutions: g(C)=0 ⇒ y=C solves the DE

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the general solution of a separable first-order differential equation.
question_archetypes.example: Solve dy/dx = xy.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The equation can be rearranged so that all y-terms (with dy) are on one side and all x-terms (with dx) are on the other — the defining feature of a separable equation.
method_plan: Rearrange to dy/g(y)=f(x)dx
Integrate both sides, adding a single constant of integration
Solve explicitly for y if possible
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct separation of variables
M1: correct integration of both sides
A1: correct solving for y (or acceptable implicit form)
A1: constant of integration correctly included and consolidated

common_errors.description: Forgetting the constant of integration, or adding two separate constants on each side instead of one combined constant
Sign or exponent errors converting ln|y|=... back to y=...
Leaving the answer in an unnecessarily implicit form when explicit solving is straightforward

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve a separable initial-value problem, using the initial condition to determine the constant and solving explicitly for y.
question_archetypes.example: Solve dy/dx=x^2y^3, y(1)=3.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: An initial condition y(x0)=y0 is given alongside the separable equation, requiring the constant to be solved for numerically before (or as part of) presenting the final explicit solution.
method_plan: Separate variables and integrate both sides with a constant C
Substitute the initial condition to solve for C
Solve explicitly for y, choosing the sign/branch consistent with the initial condition
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct separation and integration
M1: correct substitution of initial condition to find C
A1: correct algebraic solving for y
A1: correct choice of sign/branch matching the initial condition

common_errors.description: Solving for the general solution but forgetting to apply the initial condition
Errors solving −1/(2y^2)=... for y, especially the ± square root
Choosing the wrong sign/branch for y, inconsistent with the given initial value

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Identify a constant (equilibrium) solution that is lost during separation, and state it alongside the general solution.
question_archetypes.example: Solve dy/dx=y(1-y) (logistic-type) and identify any constant solutions lost during separation.
question_archetypes.answer: General solution via partial fractions: y=Ce^t/(1+Ce^t) (or equivalent); dividing by y(1-y) during separation assumed y≠0 and y≠1, so the constant solutions y=0 and y=1 must be stated separately (y=1 is recovered in the limit C→∞ of the general form here, but y=0 is genuinely a separate solution not captured for any finite C)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The right-hand side g(y) factors and has one or more real roots (values of y making g(y)=0) — these correspond to constant/equilibrium solutions that the separation step (dividing by g(y)) implicitly assumes cannot occur.
method_plan: Identify all roots of g(y)=0 before separating
Carry out the separation and integration as usual to get the general (non-constant) solution
Check whether each constant solution y=root is already included in the general solution for some choice of constant; state explicitly any that are not
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies all roots of g(y)=0 as candidate constant solutions
M1: correct general (non-constant) solution obtained
A1: correct check of whether each constant solution is captured by the general form
A1: explicitly states any constant solution missed by the general solution

common_errors.description: Dividing by g(y) without ever checking for lost constant solutions where g(y)=0
Assuming all constant solutions are automatically captured by the general solution's arbitrary constant, without verifying
Not explicitly listing the constant solution(s) alongside the general solution in the final answer

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve a separable equation whose separated form requires partial fractions to integrate (e.g. the logistic equation).
question_archetypes.example: Solve dy/dt=ky(1-y/L) for y(t) (the logistic equation).
question_archetypes.answer: L dy/(y(L-y))=k dt; partial fractions: (1/y+1/(L-y))dy=k dt ⇒ ln(y/(L-y))=kt+C ⇒ y(t)=C1Le^{kt}/(1+C1e^{kt})
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: After separating, the y-side integrand is a rational function with distinct linear factors in the denominator (like 1/(y(L-y))) — signals a partial-fractions decomposition is needed before integrating.
method_plan: Separate variables to isolate the rational function in y on one side
Decompose the rational function via partial fractions
Integrate each term (giving logarithms) and solve for y explicitly
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct separation into a rational-function integral in y
M1: correct partial fraction decomposition
A1: correct integration of each term
A1: correct final explicit solution for y(t)

common_errors.description: Attempting to integrate 1/(y(L-y)) directly without decomposing into partial fractions
Errors in the partial fraction decomposition or in solving the resulting log equation for y
Leaving the answer as an implicit log equation when the initial-value form C1Le^{kt}/(1+C1e^{kt}) is expected

micro_skills.micro_skill: Modeling with separable equations (logistic growth, mixing problems)
definitions: Many applied first-order models are separable and autonomous (rate depends only on the state, not on time): logistic population growth dy/dt=ky(1-y/L), and mixing problems where the concentration/amount x(t) satisfies dx/dt = (rate in) - (rate out), often reducing to a separable (and simultaneously linear) equation in x alone.

theorems.name: Autonomous modeling equations
theorems.statement: An autonomous first-order equation dy/dt=g(y) (no explicit t-dependence) is always separable: dy/g(y)=dt.
conditions: the modeled rate depends only on the current state y, not explicitly on t

formulas: mixing: dx/dt=(rate in)-(rate out), often (rate out)=x(t)/(volume)·(flow rate)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve a logistic growth initial-value problem and interpret the long-term behaviour of the solution.
question_archetypes.example: A population satisfies dy/dt=0.1y(1-y/500), y(0)=50. Find y(t) and describe its behaviour as t→∞.
question_archetypes.answer: Using the logistic solution form, y(t)=500/(1+9e^{-0.1t}); as t→∞, y(t)→500=L (approaches the carrying capacity)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem is explicitly framed as population/logistic growth with a given carrying capacity L and growth rate k, and (often) an initial condition, possibly also asking to describe the long-run limit.
method_plan: Recall or re-derive the general logistic solution form
Apply the initial condition to find the constant
Discuss the limit as t→∞, noting convergence to the carrying capacity L
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct application of the logistic solution formula (or re-derivation)
M1: correct use of initial condition to find the constant
A1: correct explicit y(t)
A1: correct interpretation of long-term behaviour (→L)

common_errors.description: Not recognizing y→L as t→∞ regardless of the initial population (as long as y(0)>0)
Errors applying the initial condition to solve for the constant in the logistic formula
Re-deriving the full partial-fractions solution from scratch instead of using the known logistic closed form efficiently

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Set up and solve a mixing/tank problem where a substance flows in and out of a well-mixed tank, and answer a question about the amount at a specific time.
question_archetypes.example: A 1000 L tank starts with 50 kg salt; brine at 10 g/L enters at 10 L/min, and well-mixed solution leaves at 10 L/min. Find the salt x(t) and its value at t=40.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A tank/container problem describes an inflow rate and concentration and an outflow rate (often equal, keeping volume constant), and asks to track the amount of a dissolved substance over time — set up dx/dt=(rate in)-(rate out) and solve.
method_plan: Determine the rate in (concentration × inflow rate)
Determine the rate out (current concentration = x/volume, times outflow rate)
Form dx/dt=(rate in)-(rate out), separate variables, solve using the initial condition
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct rate-in term
M1: correct rate-out term using x(t)/volume
A1: correct separation and integration
A1: correct solution and correct numeric evaluation at the requested time

common_errors.description: Using a constant outflow concentration instead of the time-varying x(t)/volume
Sign errors combining rate in and rate out into a single dx/dt expression
Forgetting to apply the initial condition, or applying it to the wrong constant after solving

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Translate a purely verbal description of a rate-of-change scenario into a separable differential equation, without necessarily solving it fully.
question_archetypes.example: The rate at which a rumor spreads through a population of size N is proportional to the product of the number who have heard it (y) and the number who haven't (N-y). Set up (but do not solve) the governing differential equation.
question_archetypes.answer: dy/dt=ky(N-y) for some proportionality constant k>0 — a logistic-type separable equation
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem is stated entirely in words (a rate 'proportional to' some product or combination of quantities), and the task is to translate this into a differential equation — a modeling/setup skill distinct from solving.
method_plan: Identify the quantity whose rate of change is being described
Translate 'proportional to (product of two quantities)' into a constant k times that product
Write the resulting differential equation, without necessarily solving
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies the dependent variable and its rate dy/dt
M1: correctly translates the verbal proportionality into the correct product form
A1: introduces an appropriate proportionality constant k
presentation: does not conflate 'setting up' with 'solving' if the problem only asks for the former

common_errors.description: Mistranslating 'proportional to the product' as a sum or a single factor instead of y(N-y)
Attempting to solve the equation when the problem only asked for the setup, wasting time
Omitting the proportionality constant k, or omitting units/context for k

micro_skills.micro_skill: Orthogonal trajectories of a family of curves
definitions: A family of curves satisfying dy/dx=F(x,y) has orthogonal trajectories — a second family of curves crossing the first at right angles everywhere — satisfying the negative-reciprocal-slope equation dy/dx=-1/F(x,y), which is often itself separable.

theorems.name: Orthogonal trajectories
theorems.statement: If a one-parameter family of curves satisfies dy/dx=F(x,y), then the family of curves orthogonal to it at every intersection satisfies dy/dx=-1/F(x,y).
conditions: F(x,y)≠0 (else the orthogonal slope is undefined/vertical, handled as a special case)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the family of orthogonal trajectories for a given family of curves, by first eliminating the parameter to get dy/dx=F(x,y).
question_archetypes.example: Find the orthogonal trajectories of the parabolas y=Cx^2.
question_archetypes.answer: Differentiating and eliminating C: dy/dx=2y/x; orthogonal equation dy/dx=-x/(2y); separating: 2y dy=-x dx ⇒ x^2+2y^2=K (family of ellipses)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A one-parameter family of curves (defined by an equation with a constant C) is given, and the task is to find the family that crosses it everywhere at right angles.
method_plan: Differentiate the family's equation and eliminate the parameter C to get dy/dx=F(x,y)
Form the orthogonal equation dy/dx=-1/F(x,y)
Solve this new (typically separable) equation for the orthogonal family
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly differentiates and eliminates C to find F(x,y)
M1: correctly forms the negative-reciprocal equation
A1: correctly separates and integrates the new equation
A1: correct final equation for the orthogonal family

common_errors.description: Forgetting to eliminate the parameter C before writing dy/dx=F(x,y), leaving C in the expression
Using the same slope F(x,y) instead of its negative reciprocal for the orthogonal family
Errors solving the new separable equation for the orthogonal family

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Verify that two given families of curves are indeed orthogonal by checking their slopes multiply to -1 at a point of intersection.
question_archetypes.example: Verify that y=Cx^2 and x^2+2y^2=K are orthogonal at their intersection point(s).
question_archetypes.answer: Slope of first family: dy/dx=2y/x; slope of second (implicit differentiation): dy/dx=-x/(2y); product = (2y/x)(-x/(2y))=-1 for all (x,y)≠(0,0), confirming orthogonality
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Two specific families/equations are given (not derived from each other in the problem) and the task is to confirm the orthogonality relationship rather than derive one family from the other.
method_plan: Find the slope (dy/dx) of each family, using implicit differentiation where necessary
Multiply the two slopes together
Confirm the product equals -1 (the condition for perpendicularity), noting any special points to exclude
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct slope for the first family
M1: correct slope for the second family (implicit differentiation)
A1: correct product of slopes shown to equal -1
A1: notes any excluded points (e.g. where a slope is undefined or zero)

common_errors.description: Errors in implicit differentiation for the second family's slope
Checking the slopes are merely equal in magnitude rather than checking their product is exactly -1
Not addressing special/excluded points where a slope is zero or undefined

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Interpret orthogonal trajectories in an applied context (e.g. equipotential lines vs. field lines, isotherms vs. heat-flow lines).
question_archetypes.example: In a 2-D steady-state temperature field, curves of constant temperature (isotherms) satisfy F(x,y)=x-y (as dy/dx). Find the differential equation for the heat-flow lines, which are orthogonal to the isotherms, and explain the physical meaning.
question_archetypes.answer: Heat-flow lines satisfy dy/dx=-1/(x-y); physically, heat flows in the direction perpendicular to lines of constant temperature (in the direction of steepest temperature change), so the flow-line family is exactly the orthogonal trajectories of the isotherm family
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem frames orthogonal trajectories using applied terminology from physics/engineering (isotherms and heat flow, equipotentials and field lines, streamlines) rather than as an abstract 'family of curves' — same math, applied interpretation required.
method_plan: Recognize the applied pair (e.g. isotherms/flow lines) as a mathematical family/orthogonal-trajectory relationship
Set up the negative-reciprocal differential equation as usual
State the physical significance of orthogonality in this applied context
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies the applied scenario as an orthogonal-trajectories problem
M1: correct negative-reciprocal equation set up
A1: correct solving if requested
A1: clear physical interpretation of why the two families are orthogonal

common_errors.description: Not recognizing the applied terminology (isotherms, equipotentials, streamlines) as literally the same orthogonal-trajectory mathematics
Solving the math correctly but omitting the requested physical interpretation
Overcomplicating the setup by not directly reusing the standard orthogonal-trajectories procedure

micro_skills.micro_skill: First-order linear equations via integrating factor
definitions: The standard form is dy/dx+p(x)y=q(x). With ρ(x)=∫p(x)dx (any antiderivative), the integrating factor e^{ρ(x)} is chosen so that d/dx(e^{ρ(x)}y)=e^{ρ(x)}(dy/dx+p(x)y)=e^{ρ(x)}q(x); integrating both sides gives y(x)=e^{-ρ(x)}∫e^{ρ(x)}q(x)dx.

theorems.name: Integrating factor method
theorems.statement: For dy/dx+p(x)y=q(x), the integrating factor μ(x)=e^{∫p(x)dx} satisfies d/dx(μy)=μq(x), so y=μ^{-1}∫μ(x)q(x)dx.
conditions: p, q continuous on the interval of interest
any antiderivative ρ=∫p dx works (the constant of integration in ρ cancels)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve a first-order linear equation given directly in standard form, using the integrating factor method.
question_archetypes.example: Solve dy/dx+y/x=1, x>0.
question_archetypes.answer: p(x)=1/x, ρ=ln x, μ=x; d/dx(xy)=x ⇒ xy=x^2/2+C ⇒ y=x/2+C/x
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The equation is given (or trivially rearranged) into the standard form dy/dx+p(x)y=q(x), signalling the integrating factor method rather than separation of variables (the equation is not separable in general).
method_plan: Identify p(x) and q(x) from the standard form
Compute ρ(x)=∫p(x)dx and the integrating factor μ=e^{ρ(x)}
Multiply through by μ, recognize the left side as d/dx(μy), integrate both sides, and solve for y
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of p(x), q(x)
M1: correct integrating factor μ(x)
A1: correct integration of μ(x)q(x)
A1: correct final solution for y, including +C

common_errors.description: Multiplying only the y-terms by μ and forgetting to multiply q(x) on the right side as well
Sign errors in ρ(x)=∫p(x)dx, which flips exponential growth/decay in μ
Forgetting the constant of integration or the final division by μ to isolate y

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve a first-order linear initial-value problem, using the integrating factor and then applying the initial condition.
question_archetypes.example: Solve dy/dx+2y=e^{-x}, y(0)=1.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: An initial condition is attached to a linear equation, requiring the constant from the integrating-factor solution to be determined numerically as a final step.
method_plan: Find the integrating factor and general solution as usual
Substitute the initial condition into the general solution to solve for C
State the particular solution
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct integrating factor and general solution
M1: correct substitution of the initial condition
A1: correct solved constant C
A1: correct final particular solution

common_errors.description: Solving the general solution correctly but forgetting to apply the initial condition
Arithmetic errors substituting x=0 (or the given point) into the general solution
Applying the initial condition to an intermediate expression (before dividing out the integrating factor) instead of to the final y(x)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Explain/derive why the integrating factor e^{∫p dx} is exactly the right choice to make the left side a perfect derivative.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why multiplying dy/dx+p(x)y=q(x) by μ(x)=e^{∫p(x)dx} turns the left side into d/dx(μy).
question_archetypes.answer: d/dx(μy)=μ'y+μy'=μp(x)y+μy' (since μ'=μp(x) by the chain rule on e^{∫p dx}) = μ(y'+p(x)y), which is exactly μ times the left side of the original equation — so multiplying through by μ makes the left side collapse to d/dx(μy)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem explicitly asks to justify/derive why the integrating factor method works (a 'show that' or 'explain why' question), not just to apply it mechanically to solve an equation.
method_plan: Differentiate the proposed μ(x)=e^{∫p dx} to find μ'(x)=p(x)μ(x)
Expand d/dx(μy) using the product rule and substitute μ'=pμ
Show the result matches μ times the original left-hand side, confirming the choice of μ was correct
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly differentiates μ using the chain rule to get μ'=pμ
M1: correctly expands d/dx(μy) via the product rule
A1: correctly matches the expansion to μ(y'+py)
A1: clear concluding statement tying this back to why the method works

common_errors.description: Treating the integrating factor as a memorized trick without being able to justify why it produces a perfect derivative
Errors differentiating e^{∫p dx} (forgetting the chain rule gives μ'=p(x)μ, not just p(x))
Jumping to 'it works' without showing the product-rule expansion connecting the two sides

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Identify and correct an error in a linear-equation solution where the integrating factor was applied only to the left side.
question_archetypes.example: A student solves dy/dx+3y=6 by finding μ=e^{3x}, then writes e^{3x}y=6+C (forgetting to multiply the right side by μ before integrating). Identify and correct the error.
question_archetypes.answer: Correct: d/dx(e^{3x}y)=6e^{3x} ⇒ e^{3x}y=2e^{3x}+C ⇒ y=2+Ce^{-3x} (not y=(6+C)e^{-3x} as the flawed version would give)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A worked solution is presented where the integrating factor multiplies the y-terms correctly but the right-hand side q(x) was left unmultiplied before integrating — a specific, common execution error to diagnose.
method_plan: Check whether the integrating factor was multiplied through the entire equation, including q(x)
Recompute the right side as ∫μ(x)q(x)dx, not just q(x) alone
Redo the final division by μ to get the corrected y(x)
full_mark_rubric: M1: identifies that q(x) was not multiplied by μ before integrating
A1: correct recomputation of ∫μq dx
A1: correct final corrected solution for y

common_errors.description: Forgetting the integrating factor must multiply the entire equation (both sides), not just the y-terms
Errors in the corrected integration of μ(x)q(x)
Not clearly showing the corrected step-by-step derivation after identifying the error

micro_skills.micro_skill: Applications of linear first-order equations (RL circuits, mixing)
definitions: An RL circuit satisfies L dI/dt+RI=V (linear, constant coefficients), giving I(t)=(V/R)(1-e^{-Rt/L}) with I(0)=0, approaching the steady-state current V/R as t→∞. Mixing problems with unequal or non-constant in/out flow rates generally give a linear (not merely separable) equation dx/dt+p(t)x=q(t), solved via the integrating factor.

theorems.name: RL circuit response
theorems.statement: For L dI/dt+RI=V with I(0)=0, I(t)=(V/R)(1-e^{-Rt/L}), with steady-state current V/R as t→∞.
conditions: L, R, V constants
I(0)=0 (initially no current)

formulas: time to reach fraction f of steady state: 1-e^{-Rt/L}=f

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve an RL circuit's linear differential equation for current, and identify the steady-state current.
question_archetypes.example: Solve L dI/dt+RI=V, I(0)=0, and find the steady-state current.
question_archetypes.answer: Integrating factor e^{Rt/L}: I(t)=(V/R)(1-e^{-Rt/L}); as t→∞, I→V/R
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem describes an electrical circuit with inductance L, resistance R, and voltage V (an RL circuit), and asks to solve for current and/or identify its long-term behaviour.
method_plan: Rewrite the circuit equation in standard linear form dI/dt+(R/L)I=V/L
Apply the integrating factor method with the initial condition I(0)=0
State the steady-state limit as t→∞
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct standard form and integrating factor
M1: correct application of the initial condition
A1: correct explicit I(t)
A1: correct identification of the steady-state current V/R

common_errors.description: Forgetting to divide through by L to get the standard form dI/dt+(R/L)I=V/L before finding the integrating factor
Errors applying I(0)=0 to solve for the constant
Not recognizing that the steady-state current is simply the t→∞ limit, obtainable without re-deriving anything once I(t) is known

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the time required for a linear-model quantity (e.g. RL current) to reach a specified percentage of its steady-state (or limiting) value.
question_archetypes.example: For L dI/dt+RI=V, I(0)=0, find the time to reach 90% of the steady-state current.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks for a specific time at which a growing/decaying quantity reaches a stated fraction or percentage of its limiting value — requires solving the exponential equation for t after already knowing the closed-form solution.
method_plan: Write the known solution I(t) in terms of its steady-state value
Set I(t) equal to the specified percentage of the steady-state value
Solve the resulting exponential equation for t using logarithms
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct expression for I(t) as a fraction of steady state
M1: correctly sets up the equation for the target percentage
A1: correct algebraic isolation of the exponential term
A1: correct final t using logarithms

common_errors.description: Errors taking the logarithm of both sides (e.g. sign errors with the negative exponent)
Confusing 'time to reach 90% of steady state' with 'time to reach 90% of the theoretical maximum I=V/R exactly' (these coincide correctly if set up properly, but sign/setup confusion is common)
Not simplifying the final logarithmic expression, or leaving R, L, symbols unsubstituted when numeric values were given

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Model and solve a mixing problem where the inflow and outflow rates differ, producing a genuinely linear (non-autonomous or variable-coefficient) equation rather than a simple separable one.
question_archetypes.example: A 500 L tank starts with 20 kg of salt. Pure water enters at 8 L/min, and the well-mixed solution leaves at 5 L/min (so volume increases over time). Set up and solve for x(t), the salt at time t.
question_archetypes.answer: Volume at time t: V(t)=500+3t. dx/dt=0-5x/(500+3t) ⇒ dx/dt+5x/(500+3t)=0, a linear (and separable) equation; integrating factor (500+3t)^{5/3} gives x(t)=20·(500/(500+3t))^{5/3}
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The inflow and outflow rates are explicitly different (so the tank's volume changes over time), making the outflow concentration's denominator a function of t rather than a constant — this generally requires the full linear-equation (integrating factor) method, even though it may also be separable in special cases.
method_plan: Track the tank's volume V(t) as a function of time given the differing in/out flow rates
Write dx/dt=(rate in)-(rate out), with rate out=x(t)/V(t)·(outflow rate)
Recognize the resulting equation's linear form and solve via the integrating factor (or separate variables if it happens to be separable)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct time-dependent volume V(t)
M1: correct differential equation for x(t) using V(t) in the denominator
A1: correct integrating factor (or separation) and integration
A1: correct final x(t) with correct constant from the initial condition

common_errors.description: Treating the tank volume as constant when the in/out flow rates actually differ
Using a constant denominator (e.g. the initial volume) throughout instead of the time-varying V(t)
Errors finding the integrating factor for a variable-coefficient equation like this one
